World.title: Germany’s modern miracle: Churches are losing believers but gaining money
World.content:
Rising salaries have outweighed the cost of hundreds of thousands leaving the church.

German commentators are calling it a modern-day “miracle.”

Hundreds of thousands of worshippers are walking away from their churches each year. The money, however, keeps rolling in.

Some 660,000 people formally quit the country’s Catholic and Protestant churches in 2025, freeing them from a levy automatically charged to registered members as a percentage of their income tax bill.

Despite the exodus, the two institutions collected more than €12.5 billion through the church tax for the 2025 fiscal year, up from around €12.4 billion in 2024.

The apparent miracle has a decidedly earthly explanation: Rising wages and Germany’s progressive tax system mean the shrinking pool of members is paying more.

“At first glance, the development may seem contradictory,” a spokesperson for the Evangelical Church in Germany — the umbrella organization representing Germany’s regional Protestant churches — said. “The reason is that church tax is calculated based on individual income tax.”





Members of Germany’s Catholic and Protestant churches and some Jewish communities pay an additional religious tax equal to 8 or 9 percent of their income tax liability, even if they don’t attend services.

In 2021, the most recent year for which comprehensive data is available, more than 29 million people paid church tax in Germany, amounting to almost half of all income taxpayers in Europe’s largest economy.

The German Finance Ministry’s 2025 payroll tax tables suggests that a single employee without children earning €50,000 gross a year pays approximately €600 in church tax annually on top of income tax, depending on the federal state. Someone earning €70,000 per year pays more than €1,000.

People are registered as part of their religious community at birth or at local government offices. To stop paying the church tax, they must formally leave through a process known as Kirchenaustritt, or “church exit.”

The procedure varies across Germany’s federal states but typically requires appearing in person at a registry office or local court to submit a declaration. Most states also charge an administrative fee.

While those who deregister can still attend services as a visitor and access some church services, they are not allowed to have a church wedding, be a godparent or be guaranteed a church burial.

In 2025, some 310,000 left the Catholic Church, while around 350,000 left one of Germany’s regional Protestant churches.

Church exit

The reasons people give for formally leaving their religious communities range from feeling less connected to the church to simply wanting to save money.

“People are leaving the Church because they feel it no longer plays a role in their lives,” said Matthias Kopp, director of communications for the German Bishops’ Conference.

“Added to this are the scandals of recent years, which have called the Church’s credibility into question,” he added. “There are also people — though this is by no means the primary reason — who leave the Church because of the church tax.”

“These are processes of alienation to which we must respond,” said Kopp.

For Jana Keil, a 33-year-old accountant from Berlin, the decision was both financial and moral. “I no longer wanted to support the system with church tax in light of the [child sex] abuse scandals,” she said.





Lukas Heinich, a 23-year-old working student, said he formally left after completing his apprenticeship because he “didn’t feel like paying the tax or supporting the church.”

That church tax revenues continue to rise despite the exodus is down to the types of taxpayers choosing to remain church members.

Those who are still paying church tax in Germany are “probably the higher earners,” said Zareh Asatryan, professor of empirical economics at the University of Münster. “Those that stay will naturally earn more income because of inflation plus real wage growth, and they will just generate more revenue.”

A miracle with an end date?

But the continued rise in church tax revenue masks significant long-term challenges — and raises questions about how long the trend can last.

While those revenues are going up, they are “relatively sluggish” and “haven’t been increasing by a lot,” said Asatryan.

The increase in revenue from the church tax is considerably lower than the increase in revenue from income tax. State revenue from wage and income taxes rose by 6.65 percent in 2025, said Kopp, whereas church tax revenue increased by 1.93 percent.

“Long-term projections indicate that church tax revenue will decline significantly over the coming decades as church membership continues to decrease,” said the spokesperson for the Evangelical Church in Germany.

Protestant churches are already preparing for their income to decrease “through long-term planning processes,” said the spokesperson. “Without this system, the church’s religious, social and charitable work would not be possible on its current scale.”

World.title: EU opens channel with Meta, TikTok to tackle Ceuta migrant crisis
World.content:
That will serve as a point of contact for platforms, fact-checkers and the Commission to quickly flag content so that it can be reviewed and taken down if necessary. The effort comes amid concerns that disinformation is promoting further crossings into the territory on Aug. 15, according to Maldita.es. Maldita.es and the European Fact-Checking Standards Network attended Monday’s meeting.

The Commission operates a rapid response system under its code of conduct on disinformation, often triggered around elections. The new mechanism on Ceuta would bring a closer group of stakeholders together, two of the people said.

Another meeting has been set for later this week, one of those people and the third person confirmed.

Meta and TikTok said they were already actively monitoring the situation in line with their policies and had set up dedicated teams to monitor and respond to content in real time.

The crisis has divided EU countries and has reignited Europe’s long-running debate on illegal migration. Italy has since been one of the harshest critics of Spain’s left-wing government and its migration policies, and has implemented border controls for travelers arriving from Spain.

Former EU commissioner Thierry Breton, who was a force behind the EU’s online content rules, on Monday said the bloc should launch a disinformation inquiry into the Ceuta crisis in an interview with Italian newspaper La Stampa.

World.title: Greece’s aging power grid blamed for catastrophic wildfires
World.content:
Two deadly wildfires in late July — one in western Attica and one on the island of Crete —were also linked to the electricity grid in preliminary findings from the Greek fire brigade. The fires destroyed more than 36,000 acres and killed four people.

“Six out of 10 major fires and 55 percent of the area burnt in 2025 were caused by the power grid,” said Elias Tziritis, wildfires actions coordinator at World Wildlife Fund Greece. “Statistically speaking, the majority of fires may not start from the power grid, but these are the ones that cause the most major, devastating fires.”

Loose or sagging power lines, vegetation coming in contact with cables, dust buildup on transmission equipment and other such faults can all generate sparks. The risk rises during strong winds and periods of heavy electricity demand, when aging infrastructure is under greater strain.

Much of Greece’s electricity grid was installed decades ago and runs above ground through fire-prone forests and increasingly depopulated rural areas. In the 1960s, the country opted for an overhead network as a cheaper way to extend electricity across the country, while the prolonged financial crisis that began in 2009 further constrained investment in the system.

Critics say Greece has moved too slowly to bury distribution lines and adapt the network to increasingly severe fire conditions.

“We raised the issue years ago, calling for something to be done with the power grid urgently,” said Christos Kalogeropoulos, a retired lieutenant-general with the Fire Service and former director of the Arson Crimes unit. “We have been calling for urgent underground cabling.”

World.title: UK approves its second weight-loss pill while EU access lags
World.content:
However, with the arrival of the first GLP-1 pill Wegovy (semaglutide) from Danish competitor Novo Nordisk — which launched in the U.S. and U.K. this year and is soon expected in some EU countries — demand for the more-convenient tablet is expected to rise.

Novo Nordisk has been attempting to reach as many patients as possible with its pill to capture market share, said CEO Mike Doustdar last week.

Doustdar also said the company would soon launch in Germany at its chosen price, ignoring pressure from the U.S. administration to raise prices in Europe.

Washington has been pressuring EU countries to pay more for medicines to offset pharma revenue losses from lower U.S. drug prices. The U.K. is the only country to agree to pay more for medicines via a bilateral deal with the U.S.

Foundayo's arrival in the U.K. will initially provide competition in the private market. A decision on whether the National Health Service will cover the pill is not expected until Nov. 18, and will be made by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence.

World.title: Europe’s scorching summer is erasing its economic growth, says report
World.content:
The biggest drag is expected to come from people struggling to work in extreme heat. Triodos estimates lost labor productivity alone could shave around 0.6 percent off EU GDP, while agricultural output could fall by between 3 and 7 percent.

“At first sight this might seem modest, but it is exactly the expected economic growth for the EU this year,” said the bank of the overall €180 billion blow.

And the summer is not over. France and Britain are bracing for their fifth heat wave of the season this week, with temperatures nearing 40 degrees Celsius in southeastern France and 36 degrees forecast in the U.K.

The bill is already mounting beyond GDP. POLITICO estimated at least 14,000 excess deaths across the six hardest-hit European countries during the record-breaking heat wave from mid-June to early July.

Drought has also hammered Europe’s energy system: Low water levels in the Danube in recent weeks have forced sharp cuts at Hungary’s Paks nuclear plant and pushed Romania to blast apart a rock to divert water toward its last operating reactor. Vessels on the Rhine and Danube have had to sail only partially loaded.

In Austria, meanwhile, drought has caused an estimated €1 billion in agricultural losses, according to Austrian Hail Insurance, after some regions received more than 75 percent less rain than normal since mid-June.

Triodos warned against treating this summer as a freak event, saying extreme heat “might become structural” as the planet warms. But governments can soften the damage through irrigation, insulation, cooling and shifting working hours, said the bank.

“Every year adaptation without mitigation is a year borrowed against a hotter baseline.”

World.title: Europe is running out of Patriot missiles as Ukraine braces for Russia’s winter attacks
World.content:
Germany, one of Ukraine’s top military aid donors, has already transferred Patriot systems and missiles to Ukraine. But Berlin must now balance Kyiv’s increasingly urgent needs against the minimum stocks required to protect Germany and meet its NATO commitments. Other European countries are also weighing whether to hang on to their interceptors or give them to Ukraine.

“We are really reaching our limits here,” Brig. Gen. Jürgen Schrödl, a senior German defense ministry official, said at a panel in Berlin shortly after last month’s NATO summit in Ankara. “We also have to ensure our own protection.”

Berlin and other Northern European capitals have urged counterparts elsewhere on the continent to examine what more military equipment and financial support they could release.

“I think it’s not sustainable for Europe in the long run,” Norwegian Defense Minister Tore O. Sandvik told POLITICO. “All the European countries have to step up.”

That's putting pressure on countries with stocks of Patriot interceptors like Poland, Spain and Greece. The shortage primarily concerns Patriot PAC-3 and PAC-2 missiles, which are among Ukraine’s few effective defenses against fast-moving Russian ballistic weapons.

Ukraine can use other, often cheaper, air-defense systems against drones and cruise missiles. The country is racing to develop its homegrown Freyja interceptor, but the anti-ballistic system still requires investment, engineering work and testing before it can fill that role.

World.title: At least 132 dead, 570 injured after Colombia quake: Cali and Pereira impose curfew
World.content:
The Colombian Association of Capital Cities reports a provisional toll of at least 132 dead and 570 injured in the departments hit by Monday's 7.4-magnitude earthquake -and its subsequent aftershocks-.

 

Cauca and Risaralda, located to the west of the so-called Coffee Axis, are the regions with the highest number of victims, according to the newspaper "El Espectador", with at least 60 and 15 deaths respectively, plus around 13 in Chocó. Other affected regions include Caldas and Quindío.

undefined

The epicentre was in San José del Palmar, in the south-east of Chocó, bordering Valle del Cauca and Risaralda and roughly equidistant from the cities of Cali and Medellín, with the former suffering the most damage to its infrastructure. Seismographs indicate that the natural disaster originated within the Nazca plate, at a depth of around 103 kilometres. This plate sinks beneath the South American plate that forms the Andes mountain range, causing friction and events of this kind.

Abelardo de la Espriella, who only recently took office as president of Colombia, travelled on Monday afternoon to Quibdó, capital of the department of Chocó, and later to Cali. As part of the reinforcement of emergency efforts, the latter city will receive 60 rescue workers from Bogotá and a further 32 members of the armed forces.

The far-right leader has announced that government representatives will head the unified command posts in the affected areas, with the departments ceding their powers on the matter. "I don't want anyone going off on their own", said the president, who will travel to the Coffee Axis in the coming days. "Information will come from the Office of the President of the Republic; from no other body of the Colombian state".

Cali and Pereira impose a curfew

The capital of Valle del Cauca has imposed a curfew between 20:00 on Monday and 6:00 on Tuesday and ordered the militarisation of the city in response to the emergency, which has left numerous structures damaged in Cali.

Mayor Alejandro Eder has justified the move as a way to allow relief agencies to focus their efforts on searching for and rescuing those people who may still be trapped under the rubble. "We are facing threats of looting, which is why I have ordered the curfew and the militarisation of Cali", Eder said, calling on citizens to report any attempted looting or incidents that threaten public safety.

undefined

His counterpart in the Colombian city of Pereira, Mauricio Salazar, also declared a curfew on Monday to prevent looting. "As of today at 18:00 we have imposed a curfew until 5:00 to protect businesses in the city. This curfew will apply in the city centre, in Comuna Universidad and in the Cuba subcentre", explained the mayor of the departmental capital of Risaralda.

In Caldas, governor Henry Gutiérrez Angel has likewise opted to impose a curfew to prevent looting and protect the population.

undefined

At the onset of the earthquake, this area suffered a blackout affecting electricity and mobile phone coverage. Up to six airports in the west of the country (Pereira, Manizales, Quibdó, Armenia, Cartago and Buenaventura) still have operations suspended. The tremor was felt in neighbouring countries far from the epicentre, such as Ecuador and Panama.

From Mexico, President Claudia Sheinbaum has expressed her solidarity with Colombia and said her country is ready to provide whatever support is needed in the emergency. Mexican media report that the Morena leader has made available to the Colombian authorities any assistance they may require.

Among those sending messages is María Corina Machado, who has conveyed her solidarity with those affected and underlined Venezuelans' experience of this type of disaster. "We know from first-hand experience how vital international solidarity is in the face of a tragedy of this magnitude", wrote the opposition leader 'de facto' in exile. This earthquake follows two consecutive quakes of magnitudes 7.2 and 7.5 off the Venezuelan coast at the end of June. Those quakes destroyed hundreds of buildings and claimed the lives of more than 5,000 people.

From Spain, Pedro Sánchez has also expressed his solidarity with the country and offered whatever assistance is needed (source in Spanish). For the time being, there are no reports of Spanish nationals among the fatalities, although the tally remains preliminary.

undefined

World.title: Explosive drone at Leipzig airport: whose DNA trail is it?
World.content:
On the night of 5 August 2026, Leipzig/Halle Airport came close to disaster when a drone fitted with explosives and a detonator appeared near a cargo aircraft operated by Ukrainian Antonov Airlines. Ammunition destined for Ukraine is reported to have been on board.

 

According to new findings, reported by the weekly Die Zeit, CCTV footage shows that at around 7.30 p.m. the drone deliberately flew towards the Ukrainian cargo aircraft and slammed into its wing. The device packed with Semtex did not explode on impact, however, but bounced off the Antonov and fell to the ground. The explosives appear to have become detached from the drone. According to Bild, the drone struck the Antonov close to the aircraft's fuel tank.

The drone was not picked up by any security system later that evening; instead, according to the report, an airport bus driver noticed the dangerous device four hours after the collision. He stepped on the drone with his foot. The explosives were apparently lying some distance away.

DNA trace on the drone apparently leads to Lithuania

Five days after the incident at Leipzig Airport, Bild and Die Zeit report that investigators have secured DNA traces on the drone that failed to explode. No individual has yet been identified, but, according to Bild, there has been a match in the European DNA database and the trail apparently leads to Lithuania.

In addition, the DNA now secured is said to match that from an arson attack on 20 July 2024 on the DHL logistics centre at Leipzig Airport. The parcel bomb exploded on the ground rather than in the air on board the aircraft only because the DHL cargo plane was delayed.

Several suspects have been on trial in the Lithuanian capital Vilnius since the spring over the 2024 parcel bomb in Leipzig. The charge is "terrorism and sabotage on behalf of a foreign power". The Lithuanian prosecutor's office stated that the offences involving improvised explosive devices had been "organised and coordinated by citizens of the Russian Federation who are linked to the military intelligence services of the Russian Federation".

The defendants are alleged to have sent parcel bombs across Europe via freight services such as DHL and DDP. According to the Lithuanian authorities, the intended targets were Germany, Poland and the United Kingdom. The EU judicial agency Eurojust in The Hague also believes Russia's military intelligence service, the GRU, was behind the 2024 wave of attacks.

Following the discovery of the drone in Leipzig, the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office is investigating on suspicion of attempted detonation of an explosive device and of endangering air traffic. Chancellor Friedrich Merz has so far avoided any hint that Russia might be responsible for the drone incident. During a visit to Leipzig, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt spoke only of the possible involvement of "foreign powers".

The Kremlin denies any involvement by Russia in the drone attack on Leipzig. On Telegram, the Russian embassy in Berlin described it as a "provocation directed against Moscow" and warned of "a new wave of anti-Russian hysteria in Germany".

World.title: 10 books, 9 films and 8 songs about eclipses
World.content:
Since Antiquity, eclipses have been interpreted as omens, as punishment or as romantic metaphors, and that fascination has left its mark on literature, cinema and music. In fact, the phenomenon has been depicted in numerous paintings, but how have eclipses influenced the most popular artistic creations?

 

Here is a look at 10 books, nine films and eight songs that, in one way or another, revolve around an eclipse.

10 books marked by an eclipse

1. 'The Odyssey' (Homer, 8th century BC) In Book 20 of the poem, the seer Theoclymenus interprets a sudden darkening of the sky as heralding the imminent death of Penelope's suitors, shortly before Odysseus confronts them.

A study published in 2008 linked that passage to a real eclipse observed in the Ionian Islands in 1178 BC. The work is currently on everyone's lips because of Christopher Nolan's film, although that episode is not mentioned in the movie.

2. The 'Song of Roland' (anonymous, 11th century) This medieval epic poem, which tells of the defeat of Roland and his army at Roncesvalles at the hands of the Saracens, describes a sudden darkening of the sky, storms and an earthquake as signs of a possible end of the world. It is a classic example of how medieval literature associated eclipses with ill omens.

3. 'A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur's Court' (Mark Twain, 1889) Hank Morgan, a mechanic from Connecticut, travels back in time to 6th-century England and is sentenced to death by burning at the stake. He then remembers that a solar eclipse is approaching and threatens to plunge the world into darkness if his life is not spared, which allows him to escape and earn a reputation as a sorcerer at King Arthur's court.

A Yankee in King Arthur's Court Anaya

4. 'King Solomon's Mines' (H. Rider Haggard, 1885) A few years before Twain, Haggard had already resorted to a very similar device: an explorer who knows the date of an imminent eclipse persuades the Kukuana tribe that he can hide the Sun with his powers, and in exchange demands that the people obey his orders.

5. Diaries (Virginia Woolf) The author of 'Mrs Dalloway' travelled in 1927 to the north of England to witness the first total eclipse visible in the country in almost 200 years. In her diaries she describes how the light disappeared completely for a few seconds and then returned all at once, which she herself noted as the most astonishing moment of the experience.

Portrait of Virginia Woolf (25 January 1882 – 28 March 1941), British writer and feminist. Wikimedia Commons

6. 'Dolores Claiborne' (Stephen King, 1992) The protagonist plans her husband's death, a violent, alcoholic man, taking advantage of the real solar eclipse that could be seen in the United States in 1963. Years later, during a police interrogation over another death, she recalls that episode to the investigators.

7. 'Gerald's Game' (Stephen King, 1992) Published in the same year as 'Dolores Claiborne', this novel also assigns a key role to the 1963 eclipse, which King used as the backdrop for two different stories told in very different tones.

8. 'Nightfall' (Isaac Asimov, 1941) On the planet Lagash, permanently lit by six suns, its inhabitants have no concept of darkness. When astronomers announce that a total eclipse will leave the planet without light for the first time in 2,000 years, society is confronted with something for which it is utterly unprepared. It is regarded as one of the best science-fiction short stories of the last century.

Nightfall Isaac Asimov

9. 'The Eclipse' (Augusto Monterroso, 1959) In this very short Guatemalan story, a Spanish friar lost in the jungle tries to save himself from being sacrificed by a group of Maya by warning them that, thanks to his knowledge, he is capable of darkening the Sun. The ironic ending turns his expectations completely on their head.

10. 'Total Eclipse' (Annie Dillard, 1982) This essay, included in the book "Teaching a Stone to Talk", recounts the author's journey to the Yakima Valley in Washington State to observe a total eclipse in 1979. Dillard describes the experience as something that completely transforms one's perception of reality, far more unsettling than she herself had expected.

Eclipse inspiration on screen

1. 'Barabbas' (Richard Fleischer, 1961) To film the crucifixion scene in this epic production, the crew timed the shoot to coincide with a real solar eclipse that took place in Italy on 15 February 1961, and deployed more than 40 cameras across Tuscany to capture the phenomenon's strange light.

2. 'Eclipse' (Michelangelo Antonioni, 1962) That same Italian eclipse of 1961 inspired Antonioni to choose the title of this film, starring Alain Delon and Monica Vitti, one of the classics of European cinema of the 1970s.

3. 'Ladyhawke' (Richard Donner, 1985) The two protagonists of this medieval fantasy, played by Michelle Pfeiffer and Rutger Hauer, are under a curse that turns her into a hawk during the day and him into a wolf at night. Only a solar eclipse, a day without night and a night without day, allows them to recover their human form at the same time.

'Ladyhawke', released in Spain as 'Lady Halcón' and under various titles in Latin America, is a fantasy, romance and adventure film directed by Richard Donner. IMDb

4. 'Apocalypto' (Mel Gibson, 2006) Set on the Yucatán peninsula in the early 16th century, the film shows its protagonist about to be sacrificed atop a Maya pyramid when a solar eclipse, interpreted by the priests as a sign from the Sun god, allows him to save his life.

5. 'Dolores Claiborne' (Taylor Hackford, 1995) A film adaptation of Stephen King's 'Dolores Claiborne', starring Kathy Bates and Jennifer Jason Leigh, which retains the central role of the 1963 eclipse in the plot.

6. 'Gerald's Game' (Mike Flanagan, 2017) Netflix's version of Stephen King's novel of the same name, starring Carla Gugino, which also brings back the 1963 eclipse as a central narrative element.

Carla Gugino in 'Gerald's Game' (2017) IMDb

7. 'Darkness' (Jaume Balagueró, 2002) In this horror thriller, a family moves into a house near Barcelona where, 40 years earlier, six children had been sacrificed in a ritual that coincided with a solar eclipse.

8. 'Venus' (Jaume Balagueró, 2022) The director of 'Darkness' once again turned to the motif of the eclipse in this film, in which a demonic entity tries to possess the protagonist, played by Ester Expósito, during the phenomenon.

9. 'Verónica' (Paco Plaza, 2017) Set during the 1991 solar eclipse in Madrid, the protagonist holds a seance with a ouija board in the middle of the phenomenon, with consequences that shape the rest of the film.

Eclipse in music

1. 'Total Eclipse of the Heart', Bonnie Tyler (1983) Written and produced by Jim Steinman, it became the biggest hit of the Welsh singer's career and a classic that gets played every time there is an eclipse anywhere in the world. Tyler died last July at the age of 75, just a few weeks before this eclipse, which her song has ended up turning into the phenomenon's unofficial anthem. Link:

2. 'Eclipse', Pink Floyd (1973) The track closes the album 'The Dark Side of the Moon' with a melody that builds to a climax and ends with the same heartbeat that opens the record, thus completing the circle of the whole album. Link:

3. 'You're So Vain', Carly Simon (1972) In one of its most memorable verses, the singer tells how the song's protagonist flies by private jet to Nova Scotia, in Canada, to witness a total solar eclipse, one of pop's most frequently cited references to this phenomenon. Link:

4. 'Eclipse Total del Amor', Lissette (1984) A Spanish-language version of 'Total Eclipse of the Heart', recorded by Cuban singer Lissette for her album 'Caricatura', with its own lyrics that depart in part from the original and that became a hit in Spanish-speaking countries. Link:

5. 'Eclipse' (feat. Los Macorinos), Natalia Lafourcade (2018) Included on 'Musas, Vol. 2', the album in which the Mexican singer pays tribute to Latin American folk music together with guitar duo Los Macorinos, this song uses the image of a lunar eclipse to describe the sadness of heartbreak. Link:

6. 'Eclipse de Luna', Luciano Pereyra (2000) A track from the Argentine singer's album 'Recordándote' that uses the image of a lunar eclipse as a metaphor for a night of passion. Link:

7. 'Total Eclipse', Klaus Nomi (1981) The German singer and countertenor, one of the most singular figures of New York post-punk, turned the eclipse into a metaphor for a nuclear catastrophe in this song, one of the most memorable tracks of his career, which he first performed at the festival "Urgh! A Music War" in 1980. Link:

8. 'Bad Moon Rising', Creedence Clearwater Revival (1969) Written by John Fogerty, it does not speak of an eclipse in the strict sense, but its lyrics about earthquakes, storms and dire omens under a menacing moon have made it a regular feature of playlists devoted to astronomical phenomena and dark portents. Link:

Bonus track

'Eclipse', Delta Goodrem (2026) The Australian singer represented her country at Eurovision 2026 with this track, written together with Jonas Myrin, Ferras Alqaisi and Michael Fatkin, which uses the image of an eclipse as a metaphor for a love that aligns two different worlds in a perfect instant.

The video, shot on the dunes of Newcastle, stages that crossing between light and shadow. The song reached the final of the festival, held in Vienna, where it finished in fourth place. Link:

At Euronews we will be offering live coverage of the eclipse, so if you cannot get to the eclipse path in Spain, or if you are outside Spain, we invite you to join us to experience the total solar eclipse, a rare event that has not occurred in the Iberian Peninsula for more than 100 years.

World.title: What is the EU doing to tackle its growing water scarcity?
World.content:
Water is under stress when we use 20 percent of renewable freshwater resources, and severely stressed at 40 per cent, according to the European Environmental Agency (EEA)’s Water Exploitation Index Plus (WEI+). Today, 30 percent of Europeans and 20 percent of land face water scarcity each year, according to the European Commission.

 

Current temperatures deepen Europe's water crisis as heat dries soils and shrinks rivers. Behind the heat lies a water system already pushed to its limits. Decades of pollution, overuse, and resource mismanagement have harmed water bodies, leaving the EU with few reserves to fight today’s water crisis.

The EU launched the Water Resilience Strategy in June 2025 to make the EU water-resilient. It protects the water cycle, promotes a water-smart economy, and ensures access to clean, affordable water.

“Water is no longer just an environmental investment. It is an investment in people’s wellbeing, Europe’s food security, public health, economic competitiveness and resilience. And if Europe underinvests in water today, it will not be institutions that feel the consequences first, it will be ordinary people”, said Thomas Bajada, MEP of the Progressive Alliance of Socialists and Democrats (S&D) and rapporteur of the Water Resilience Strategy in the European Parliament.

Why are Europe’s water resources drying up?

Water stress happens for different reasons. Europe relies heavily on water for farming, industry, and energy production, leading to resource overuse. The EEA reports that total abstractions decreased by 14 percent from 2000 to 2023, but the EU still draws around 200,000 cubic metres annually, often exceeding natural replenishment rates. This depletes river flows and groundwater, leaving less water across the system. Emerging water-intensive industries, including semiconductors and data centres, consume water reserves even faster. While wastewater reuse can cut abstractions, Europe recycles only 2.4 percent of it.

Europe wastes 23 percent of treated water because of poor management of public supply networks, which reduces supply. “Across the Union, we are still losing enormous volumes of treated drinking water through ageing pipes before it even reaches people’s taps”, Bajada warned.

The 2026 EurEau report shows a slight reduction in Europe’s water losses to approximately 23.5 percent, compared with 24 percent in the 2021 survey, but member states still don’t invest enough in infrastructure maintenance. Germany leads with €9 billion annually, France with €6.5 billion, while Slovenia invests only approximately €100 million. Increased urbanisation and migration will raise water demand, especially in Northern and Western Europe, pushing for infrastructure modernisation and expansion, the European Parliamentary Research Service (EPRS) reports.

Climate change intensifies this trend. In Europe, temperatures are rising by 0.56 degrees Celsius per decade, higher than the global average of 0.27 degrees Celsius, as reported by Copernicus, the EU’s Earth observation programme.Droughts have increased, affecting 601,193 square kilometres of land, and damaging 33,518 square kilometres of forest and 87,567 square kilometres of cropland in 2024. The EEA reports that by 2050, droughts will intensify, increasing water evaporation.

Share of land area exposed to drought, EU27, 2025-2026

As reserves decline, pollution worsens, reducing clean, usable water. “Groundwater quality can be affected by climate change through interdependencies between pollution and over-abstraction. For example, if an aquifer is over-abstracted, the concentrations of nutrients and chemicals may increase because pollutants will be less diluted”, the EEA told Euronews.

The Water Resilience Strategy

“The Water Resilience Strategy changes one very important thing: it changes how we think about water”, said Bajada. It secures Europe’s long-term water supply through more than 50 actions. Its Actions Tracker monitors implementation and reports that 3 are now complete.

The strategy addresses over-abstraction and soil degradation by protecting the quantity and quality of the water cycle. The “sponge facility” restores ecosystems' ability to retain, purify, and release water, supporting biodiversity. Shared water-scarcity indicators and early warnings monitor water availability and drought risks, enhancing preparedness.

To ensure quality, the strategy reduces water pollution and removes pollutants from drinking water, protecting public health. A stronger implementation of the Water Framework Directive improves the ecological health of rivers and lakes.

The “water efficiency first" principle targets a water-smart economy that minimises water waste before turning to new sources, such as desalination. The EU targets a 10 percent increase in water efficiency by 2030 through water reuse in agriculture, industry, and public water supply. It limits water needs for clean industrial and digital sectors through smart planning, reduces leakage and water losses in public water supply, and strengthens water controls.

The Digital Action Plan on water modernises water management through data-driven tools such as smart metering, AI forecasting, satellite-based soil moisture monitoring, digital irrigation, and leak detection systems.

The 10 percent target is a strong political signal, not the final goal, Bajada said. Climate change affects European regions differently, so one target cannot suit all, he explained, calling for sector-specific efficiency and basin-level goals that consider diverse water uses and risks across agriculture, industry, public supply, and energy.

The last pillar of the strategy encourages the use of water-efficient products through the Ecodesign Regulation and supports water pricing based on usage and ability to pay, ensuring fair access and promoting smarter water-saving habits. Member states must inform citizens about national water conditions and their management for public participation in national water plans.

For Bajada, the European Investment Bank’s €15 billion investment in the strategy “is a very important step” but “it is not enough to match the scale of Europe’s water challenge”. Water resilience, he explained, means that families continue to have running water and farmers can keep producing food despite longer droughts. This is why Bajada pushes for a dedicated water resilience budget and for water to remain a priority in the next Multiannual Financial Framework.

Which countries suffer most?

Southern Europe remains the driest. Its hot, dry climate increases water demand, mainly in agriculture, pushing the region to use most of its freshwater and all of it during the hottest months.

In 2023, water scarcity hit 28 percent of land and 32 percent of Europeans, according to the EEA 2025 report. In Southern Europe, 30 percent of the population faces permanent water stress, rising to 70 percent during summer when water demand from tourism, agriculture, and public use increases. In response, the region extracts large quantities of non-replenished fossil groundwater, further straining groundwater reserves.

Cyprus and Malta suffer the most. Latest data show that Cyprus used 92.1 percent of its freshwater and Malta 66.7 percent in 2023, both exceeding the WEI+ 40 percent threshold. Between 2020 and 2024, drought impact in Cyprus rose to 12.9 percent of Cyprus’s territory and 57.1 percent of Malta (up from 6.5 percent in 2020), according to the EEA.

Seasonal water scarcity conditions for European countries in 2023, measured by the water exploitation index plus (WEI+)

To face scarcity, Cyprus reuses almost 100 percent of its wastewater, while Malta reuses only 5-10 percent. Both islands have expanded their desalination plants, which provide almost all of their drinking water.

Northern and Central Europe face a different type of water pressure but remain below the WEI+ water-stress threshold. In 2023, WEI+ scores were 0.3 percent in Sweden, 4.4 percent in Germany, and 8 percent in Poland, driven mainly by water demand from the industrial and energy sectors. The EEA reports that switching to water-efficient cooling systems and fuels, using technological innovations, and using waste heat from power plants could reduce water abstraction by up to 95 percent.

What water scarcity means for you

Electricity accounts for 33 percent of overall abstraction. “Low discharges in rivers may affect water-dependent electricity production in thermal and nuclear power plants or hydropower facilities and reduce the depth of water in free-flowing rivers, affecting inland shipping”, the EEA explained. Power plants can scale back or shut down entirely, impacting energy supply for citizens and industries, as is currently happening in Hungary and Romania. In Sweden, the Ringhals nuclear plant had to suspend its operations in July 2018 as seawater temperatures reached 25 degrees Celsius.

Agriculture uses 31 percent of Europe’s water. Shortages lead to smaller harvests, exposing farmers to health and economic losses and disrupting food supply chains. Crop losses already fell by more than 30 percent over the last decade compared to predicted trends, the EPRS reports. This can cause long-term inflation in food prices.

Total water abstraction by economic sector between 2000-2009, 2010-2019 and 2020-2023 in EU27

21 percent of total abstractions are for public water supply. This is where citizens feel the impact of water shortages most as national governments limit water use for activities such as washing, sanitation, cooking, and gardening. Cuts hit Mediterranean regions harder, as tourists increase water use by 300 to 2,000 litres per person per day, compared with residents' 125 litres, according to the EEA.

“While large cities generally have drought preparedness plans and prioritise drinking water supply, smaller municipalities and households relying on private wells are often more vulnerable to water scarcity conditions. In some countries, a significant share of the population depends on private water sources, which are less regulated and more susceptible to water scarcity”, the EEA told Euronews.

Industrial production uses 14 percent of the EU’s total water. Shortages disrupt water-intensive sectors, such as steel, paper, and food, causing shutdowns. They reduce companies’ revenues, hinder loan repayments, and trigger instability in the banking system. The European Central Bank found that 34 percent of euro-area business loans finance water-intensive sectors.

World.title: Mapping the past: Cappadocia Biennial charts new course between art and geography
World.content:
This year, Cappadocia is attracting attention not only with its unique landscape that welcomes millions of people, but also with the space it's opening up for contemporary art.

 

The first Cappadocia Biennial, spread across different parts of the region, takes visitors beyond a traditional exhibition by placing art within valleys, rock-hewn structures and settlements bearing the traces of centuries. In this way, the biennial turns from an event where works are simply viewed into a route that is lived by walking and experienced by exploring.

Extending across Göreme, Ürgüp, Avanos, Uçhisar, Ortahisar, Mustafapaşa and Kayaşehir in Nevşehir, the biennial transforms Cappadocia's natural and historical fabric into an exhibition space. This choice makes it almost impossible to think about the works independently of their surroundings. Works encountered inside a cave, between stone walls or in the silence of the valleys carry not only their own narratives but also the memory of the place.

Sude Irmak Hekimoğlu & Toprak Sencer - Migration Buse Keskin/Euronews

The biennial, brought to life by the creative art collective Sinemasal, takes the theme of "Birth" in its first edition as a metaphor for individual and social transformation. Its curatorial approach invites us to see art not merely as a field of aesthetic expression, but to think about and seek solutions to issues such as natural disasters, wars, economic crises, migration and inequality. Basic needs such as housing, food, education and healthcare also become one of the shared areas of discussion within the works.

Begüm Macan - Earth Memory Buse Keskin/Euronews

One of the most striking aspects when visiting the biennial is that the theme of "Birth" is not confined to a single interpretation. Photographs, videos, installations, AI-assisted productions and works created with natural materials all approach the same concept from very different angles.

Some invite us to reflect on migration and belonging, while others focus on nature, the memory of stone or the human imagination. Thus, at every stop, visitors encounter a different layer of the same theme.

Doğa Başaran - Kaftan Buse Keskin/Euronews

Cappadocia itself becomes an important part of this narrative. The region's timeless feel, its caves, stone structures and natural landscape do not simply provide a backdrop surrounding the works; they become an element that completes them.

Many pieces establish such a strong spatial relationship that they would not have the same impact if moved to another setting. This is precisely where one of the biennial's strongest aspects comes to the fore: the works do not merely borrow Cappadocia's spirit, they coexist with it.

Nurhayat Varol - Algorithmic World Buse Keskin/Euronews

Interactive works are also among the elements that reinforce this experience. In some pieces, the audience ceases to be merely observers and becomes part of the production or the narrative. This ensures that the participatory approach advocated by the biennial does not remain at the level of theory, but is directly reflected in the visitor's experience.

Cappadocia is already one of Turkey's most popular tourist destinations. By adding a new layer to the region, the biennial has enormous potential to strengthen cultural tourism. Encountering artworks while walking through the valleys feels less like visiting an exhibition and more like following a route of discovery. In this respect, the biennial suggests rereading Cappadocia not only through its natural beauty, but also through the relationship it builds with contemporary art.

Kaoru Shibuta - Sonic Futurity Buse Keskin/Euronews

With its first edition, the Cappadocia Biennial has made a very strong start with its choice of venues and experience-oriented approach. If it can increase its international visibility in the coming years, it looks set to seal its place among Turkey's new biennials, but also become a major international meeting point where contemporary art and cultural heritage come together on the same ground.

World.title: Low water: the story behind the Wehrmacht motorbike from the Danube
World.content:
The water level in the Danube has never been this low. The low water has revealed what lay hidden on the riverbed for decades, including a Wehrmacht motorcycle of the DKW NZ 350-1 type from the Second World War. DKW stands for the abbreviation of "Dampfkraftwagen", a former German car and motorcycle brand from the Saxon motor city of Zschopau that was later taken over by Auto Union.

 

Low water level: Wehrmacht motorcycle found in the mud of the Danube in the heart of Budapest. (c) Volksbund Volksbund

The motorcycle was found in the riverbed in the centre of Hungary's capital, Budapest, at the level of the Hungarian Parliament building. For staff at the local Institute and Museum of Military History, it is a genuine once-in-a-century find. The vehicle is almost completely intact, the institute reports. It was preserved in the Danube's mud.

DKW racing motorcycles from 1939 and 1931, archive Copyright 2007 AP. All rights reserved.

The motorcycle recovered is a model developed specifically for the war and produced from 1944 onwards. It was equipped with a two-stroke engine producing 11.5 hp. Their robustness and reliability made these bikes popular with the troops. The DKW 350-1 is easy to recognise by the metal pannier mounted on the side – a feature also found on the bike from the Danube.

Around 12,000 units were built by the end of the war in 1945. According to the ADAC, the predecessor model, the DKW (source in German) NZ 350, had a top speed of 105 km/h. Within the Wehrmacht, motorcycles were used primarily as dispatch, reconnaissance or courier vehicles.

German troops driving through Liège in Belgium, 30 May 1940 AP

The motorcycle was built by Auto Union AG, a car and motorcycle manufacturer founded in 1932 and, at the time, the second-largest producer after Opel. Auto Union AG was formed by merging several marques, including Audi.

On earlier models from the manufacturer, the frame parts were still bolted together. On the NZ series they were welded. Because this required a high power supply, the welding could only be carried out at night, when the grid was not under other strain.

German Teller mines 35, used against tanks at the time, as well as remnants of hand grenades and artillery shells, have also been found on the bed of the Danube. This stretch of the river may have been used as a "war debris dump", according to Hungary's Military History Institute.

On 2 August the motorcycle was discovered on the Buda side of the Hungarian Parliament – next to the harbour at Batthyány Square. Volksbund Volksbund

From March 1944 German troops besieged Budapest. Between October 1944 and February 1945 this culminated in the Battle of Budapest between the Soviet Red Army and German and Hungarian forces. Around 30,000 German, more than 17,000 Hungarian and about 80,000 Soviet and Romanian soldiers were killed. On 13 February 1945 the remaining German units surrendered.

After the war, DKW's production facilities were dismantled and taken to the Soviet Union as part of reparations. In Moscow and other locations, they were used until 1951 to manufacture, in large numbers, the largely identical ISCH-350.

Human remains were found beneath the motorcycle. The Volksbund Deutsche Kriegsgräberfürsorge (German War Graves Commission) took charge of the recovery and says the remains belong to two Wehrmacht soldiers. The crew of the motorcycle? Their identity tags are well preserved, so they should be identifiable. The two dead men are to be buried at the German war cemetery in Budaörs, west of Budapest. More than 16,000 German soldiers are buried there.

The Volksbund is a non-profit association which, on behalf of the federal government, searches for, recovers and buries war dead abroad. In 2025 alone, it handled more than 5,500 cases.

World.title: Russia's Supreme Court bars anti-war party Yabloko from parliamentary elections
World.content:
Russia's Supreme Court on Monday annulled the only liberal, anti-war party party Yabloko' registration for the country's parlimentary vote also known as the State Duma elections.

 

The ruling, which sidelines the only officially registered party that opposes Moscow's war ‌in Ukraine, came after the pro-Kremlin nationalist Rodina party filed a lawsuit on 7 August, seeking to remove Yabloko from the elections.

Reacting to the decision at the Supreme Court of the Russian Federation, Yabloko leader Nikolai Rybakov said that "there are no grounds at all for removing the party from the elections."

Rybakov stressed that "all the documents had been checked by the Central Election Commission, and the decision to allow us to run was taken unanimously", recalling that the Justice Ministry had repeatedly inspected the party for various violations but found nothing illegal.

He described Rodina's claims as unsubstantiated and groundless.

Dozens of people came to the Supreme Court building in Moscow to show support for Yabloko.

Rodina leader and State Duma deputy Alexei Zhuravlyov argued that "lawyers have found numerous violations" in Yabloko's election campaign.

According to him, "first and foremost this is foreign funding that does not go through the account", as well as "extensive activity on banned social networks, which is financed from the West".

Zhuravlyov also accused Yabloko of extremism. Rodina said it saw "signs of extremism" in Yabloko's call for peace.

But Rodina was not the only party to oppose Yabloko. Leaders of other Russian parties also levelled accusations against Yabloko.

Chair of the Central Committee of the Communist Party of the Russian Federation Gennady Zyuganov blamed his opponents for not supporting "the policy of strengthening Russian statehood" and for having "never once condemned the actions" of the Ukrainian authorities.

While LDPR leader Leonid Slutsky called for Yabloko to be designated an undesirable organisation because of its proposal to enter into peace talks with Kyiv.

Sergei Mironov, leader of A Just Russia, said that the Justice Ministry and the Prosecutor General's Office should "take a close look at Yabloko because the party 'opposes the special military operation', 'promises to conclude a peace that would disgrace the country' and 'supports foreign agents'".

Russia's Central Election Commission registered Yabloko's federal list for the elections to the Russian parliament on 29 July. The party decided to run under the slogan "For peace and freedom."

An anti-war party in Russia's parliamentary elections

Yabloko's election programme, made up of just 43 words, contains a call for "a ceasefire agreement, diplomacy, and the achievement of peace!"

For many, the registration of a party that advocates ending the war came as a surprise and has prompted much speculation about how and why this could have happened.

"A source close to the Central Election Commission believes that the logic behind allowing it is likely this: the authorities need a channel through which citizens can 'vent' their discontent. Better into Yabloko than into spoiling ballot papers or voting for the Communist Party," Important Stories writes.

"Yabloko was registered according to a plan by the Presidential Administration. After the elections, the party's low official result can be presented as the share of Russians who oppose the war," Radio Liberty quotes political analyst Ivan Preobrazhensky as saying.

Another widely circulated claim or belief is that Yabloko's appearance on the ballot paper is needed by the Russian authorities to take part of the vote away from the increasingly popular New People party. "Yabloko has been let into the elections to take down 'New People'," writes Alexander Kynev, a specialist in Russia's regional political processes, on social media.

Elections to the State Duma, along with various votes at different levels held at the same time, will take place in Russia over three days, from 18 to 20 September.

World.title: Germany news: Rhine levels could cause production cuts
World.content:
08/11/2026 August 11, 2026 Low water in Rhine will cause production cuts — IW research institute

Cargo ships on the Rhine are carrying only around a fifth of their normal loads Image: Oliver Berg/dpa/picture alliance

The reduction in cargo being shipped via the Rhine because of low water levels will lead companies to cut production, a leading economic research institute reports.

"Transport routes south of Kaub are now threatening to become completely severed, meaning the Rhine is cut in two," Thomas Puls, the transport expert from the German Economic Institute (IW) told the daily Rheinische Post.

"Because neither road nor rail are able to take the goods needed, the most likely reaction of primary industries will be to reduce production," he said.

This assessment appeared to be confirmed by a spokesman for the chemical company Covestro, who told the paper that the shortfalls in supply caused by the disruption to Rhine shipping was already affecting production.

The spokesman said that the current lifting of a ban on trucks using the motorway on Sundays would be of only temporary benefit.

"Ship transport via the Rhine can barely be compensated on the road, as a cargo vessel that can carry 1,500 tons is the equivalent of around 60 trucks," he said. "So ship transport cannot be completely shifted to roads."

The record low water levels on the Rhine caused by a prolonged shortage of rainfall in Germany mean that ships are currently able to carry only around a fifth of the load they usually transport.

World.title: Middle East: Trump took secret flight out of Turkey over Iran threat
World.content:
Skip next section Trump took secret flight out of Turkey over Iran threat — report

08/11/2026 August 11, 2026 Trump took secret flight out of Turkey over Iran threat — report

US President Donald Trump reportedly departed from Turkey on a secret military flight in July, instead of the flying aboard an older Air Force One plane as announced by the White House.

This was in response to a credible Iranian assassination threat, the Washington Post reported, as the monthslong war continued.

Trump had taken the newly renovated Qatari-donated jet to Ankara for the NATO summit in July. However, he unexpectedly announced he would used an older Air Force One when departing the country, "for old times's sake." The move had then raised question over the donated jet's safety.

Trump boarded the older Air Force One in front of cameras but was secretly shuttled by an airport catering truck to a smaller plane, an Air Force C-32A, the Washington Post said, citing corroborating material and a US official familiar with the operation.

Journalists aboard the decoy Air Force One, where they believed to be accompanied by the US President, said they had been advised to keep their window shades closed in the press cabin.

When they inquired about it later, Trump said it was because they were "probably on a dangerous flight."

"But if I go, you go. Right?" he added.

The White House did not directly address the report.

Communications director Steven Cheung told the Post there were "many enemies of America" targeting Trump and that every available tool was being used tocounter threats.

World.title: Trump pushes overhaul of US policy on vaccines for children
World.content:
In an executive order, President Trump calls for fewer recommended childhood vaccinations and more spacing between shots. Medical experts say the changes lack scientific backing and could leave children less protected.

On Monday, President Donald Trump signed an executive order seeking sweeping changes to the US's childhood vaccine policy, including fewer recommended immunizations and more separate appointments for children to receive them.

The order calls for the combined measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, known as MMR, to be separated into three single-disease shots. It also advocates administering childhood immunizations at separate medical visits whenever possible.

A healthcare worker prepares an MMR vaccination at a health center in Texas [FILE: April 8, 2025] Image: Annie Rice/AP Photo/picture alliance

Trump described the move as a "major victory for parents rights, religious and constitutional rights, and for the gold standard science."

What changes does Trump want for childhood vaccines?

The order says the federal government will support 11 core childhood vaccinations and advises states and territories to review vaccine requirements for school enrollment.

However, Washington cannot directly determine most school vaccine mandates, which are largely set by individual states. On those requirements, Trump's order is therefore primarily a recommendation.

The order also directs the Health and Human Services Department to improve vaccine research and develop a plan to make separate measles, mumps and rubella vaccines available in the US. Such single-antigen vaccines are not currently licensed there.

US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has long questioned established vaccine recommendations and promoted a disproven link between vaccines and autism Image: Andrew Leyden/ZUMA/picture alliance

Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. had already sought in January to remove vaccines against six of 17 diseases from the childhood schedule. A federal judge later blocked those changes while legal proceedings continue. Monday's order reaffirms much of that overhaul.

Why do experts oppose spacing out vaccines?

Public health experts say childhood vaccination schedules are based on extensive research into when and how vaccines can safely be administered together. Safety monitoring continues after vaccines are introduced.

They warn that spreading shots across more appointments can leave children vulnerable to preventable diseases for longer and increase the risk that later doses are delayed or missed.

Vaccine maker Merck said there was no published scientific evidence showing any benefit from splitting the MMR vaccine. Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics, estimated that developing and approving separate vaccines in the US could take more than a decade.

"We're advising that you continue to give children a vaccine that has decades of safety data," said Aaron M. Milstone, a member of the AAP Committee on Infectious Diseases.

What does Trump say about vaccines and autism?

Speaking in the Oval Office, Trump repeatedly suggested that the number or timing of childhood vaccines could be linked to rising rates of autism spectrum disorder.

Scientific consensus and decades of studies have found no link between vaccination and autism.

Kennedy has also repeatedly promoted the disproven connection. He founded an anti-vaccine nonprofit before joining the administration.

How have experts reacted to Trump's vaccine order?

Republican Senator Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, a physician and chairman of the Senate health committee, condemned the move.

"I'm a doctor. This executive order is wrong. The president does not have the expertise to make these changes," Cassidy said, adding that splitting combination vaccines "will mean children have to get more shots to get the same protection, not fewer shots."

Republican Senator Bill Cassidy, a physician, has sharply criticized Trump's executive order on childhood vaccines, saying it could leave children less protected [FILE: May 19, 2026] Image: Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call/Sipa USA/picture alliance

Cassidy cast the decisive vote to confirm Kennedy as health secretary in 2025 despite concerns over his vaccine skepticism. He lost his Republican primary in May to a Trump-backed challenger and is due to leave office in January.

New York City Health Commissioner Alister Martin said the order was based "in politics and conspiracy theories."

"Fortunately, vaccination recommendations are not set by the president, nor should they be," Martin said.

Why is the timing of Trump's vaccine push significant?

The policy shift comes as the United States experiences its worst measles outbreak in 35 years and children prepare to return to school.

Critics have accused Kennedy of contributing to vaccine hesitancy through years of questioning established immunizations.

The renewed focus on vaccines also marks a shift from the administration's recent emphasis on less divisive health policies, including healthy eating, drug price negotiations and efforts to combat medical fraud ahead of November's midterm elections.

Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah

World.title: Turkey MPs back historic law on reintegrating PKK militants
World.content:
Turkey's parliament has taken a major step toward ending four decades of conflict with the PKK. The new law sets out how some militants can return to civilian life, but leaves Abdullah Ocalan's future unresolved.

Turkey's parliament on Monday approved legislation offering a conditional pardon and legal protections to thousands of members of the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK).

After around 12 hours of debate, lawmakers voted 468 to 88 in favor of the 12-article bill, with six abstentions. It was backed by President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's AK Party, its nationalist MHP allies and the pro-Kurdish DEM party.

What does Turkey's new PKK law provide?

The law sets out procedures for the PKK's disarmament and dissolution and the reintegration of some members into civilian life. The government has stressed that it is not a general amnesty.

Some prison sentences would be suspended, while investigations and trials could be postponed for five or 10 years depending on the offense.

If those covered commit no terrorism-related crime during that period, cases would be dropped and sentences considered served.

Turkish lawmakers debated the bill for around 12 hours before voting on the legislation Image: Mustafa Kaya/Xinhua/picture alliance

Around 3,500 PKK-linked detainees could initially be released, lawmakers said. Media reports suggest exiled members and fighters in Iraq and Syria could also benefit.

People convicted of intentional killings and some serving life sentences are excluded.

When will the law take effect?

The measures will only come into force once Turkey's National Security Council confirms that the PKK has dissolved and surrendered all weapons.

Those seeking to benefit would then have six months to apply. Ministerial and parliamentary committees are also due to monitor the process.

Turkish Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz hailed the vote as a 'historic step' toward ending the decades-long conflict with the PKK [FILE: March 27, 2026] Image: Ahmet Okur/Anadolu Agency/IMAGO

Turkey’s Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz called the vote a "historic step", saying "the 468 'yes' votes are of the utmost importance in terms of political consensus".

What happens to Abdullah Ocalan?

The law does not cover imprisoned PKK founder Abdullah Ocalan, 77, who has been held on Imrali island near Istanbul since 1999.

Yilmaz said Ocalan's case "does not fall within the scope of this law", but added that he could remain "in a position to contribute to the peace process".

Ocalan has been central to the initiative. In February 2025, he urged the PKK to disarm and dissolve and pursue Kurdish rights through democratic means.

This latest image of imprisoned PKK founder Abdullah Ocalan was provided by the pro-Kurdish DEM party [FILE: February 27, 2026] Image: DEM

The PKK announced its dissolution in May 2025. Two months later, militants symbolically burned weapons at a ceremony in northern Iraq and the group said it was withdrawing fighters from Turkey.

What does the PKK say?

The PKK has called the legislation a "beginning" but said it contains "serious shortcomings and deficiencies."

It has demanded Ocalan's release and said the process can move forward only if he "lives and works freely."

The group also said fighters would not return without guarantees that they could engage in politics without prosecution over their views or organizations.

Pro-Kurdish DEM lawmaker Gulistan Kilic Kocyigit said: "The people of Turkey, who have paid a heavy price for many years, now have an opportunity to consolidate peace and build democracy."

Why is the bill controversial?

Nationalist opposition lawmakers accuse the government of making concessions to the PKK.

"How can you negotiate with terrorists? You said they would be laying down their weapons unconditionally," said Turhan Comez, a lawmaker with the nationalist opposition Iyi party.

Turkey: An end to the Kurdish conflict? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Iyi Party leader Musavat Dervisoglu also said the law "would pave the way" for Erdogan to remain in power. Erdogan could run again if parliament calls an early election during his current term.

Why does the conflict matter?

The PKK launched its insurgency in 1984. More than 40,000 people have been killed, and the conflict has caused major economic damage in Kurdish-majority southeastern Turkey and fueled decades of political and social division.

The PKK initially sought an independent Kurdish state but later shifted toward demands for autonomy and expanded rights.

It is designated a terrorist organization by Turkey, the United States and the European Union.

Previous peace efforts failed, most recently in 2015.

The initiative could also have regional effects, including closer Turkish-Iraqi ties and implications for efforts to integrate areas in Syria administered by the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) with Damascus.

The SDF's dominant militia, the People's Defense Units (YPG), is seen as an offshoot of the PKK, and is considered by Ankara to be a terrorist organization.

World.title: Russia: Top court bans opposition anti-war party from vote
World.content:
Yabloko, Russia's only anti-war party, has been barred from September's parliamentary elections. The motion to bar Yabloko was filed by the nationalist pro-Kremlin party Rodina.

The Supreme Court of Russia on Monday ruled in favor of the nationalist pro-Kremlin Rodina (Motherland) party and barred Yabloko (Apple) — Russia's only anti-war party — from participating in September parliamentary elections.

Rodina accuses Yabloko of receiving undeclared financial support from Western sources, among other things.

Arguing before the court, Yabloko vehemently denied the accusations and railed against Rodina's lack of supporting evidence.

The nationalist pro-Kremlin Rodina party brought the case, accusing Yabloko of receiving foreign funding, yet without providing evidence to support the claim Image: Pavel Seleznev/TASS/picture alliance

On Monday, Judge Vyacheslav Kirillov said, "The claims seeking to annul the registration of the federal list of candidates for the State Duma of the ninth convocation, nominated by the Yabloko political party, were granted."

The court's decision means citizens opposed to Russia's four-and-a-half-year invasion of Ukraine — or "special military operation" as it has been legally deemed under penalty of imprisonment — have no opportunity to vote for representatives willing to articulate that opposition.

Yabloko leader Nikolay Rybakov told the hundred or so supporters gathered outside the court, "Excluding Yabloko from the election means refusing dialog with people who ask questions that are uncomfortable for the authorities."

"We have a long road ahead and we have a big and important task — to stop deaths and bring back peace. Everything we do should be dedicated to that," Rybakov added, vowing to appeal the decision.

Yabloko — the only liberal party still operating in Russia since most of President Vladimir Putin's opponents have been jailed, exiled or murdered — has received the backing of several exiled opposition figures, including Yulia Navalnaya, the widow of the late opposition leader Alexei Navalny.

Yabloko was once a strong liberal force in Russia but like other opposition outfits it has been systematically sidelined by the Kremlin.

The party is currently only polling around three percent — short of the five percent threshold for entry into parliament — and has not won a seat in the federal State Duma since 2003.

Putin-backing United Russia has won every single election since then and that is expected to again be the case in September.

Yabloko supporters ignored the threat of repression to show support for the party's anti-war stance at the Supreme Court Image: Yevgeny Messman/TASS/picture alliance

But despite barring political opposition to the war, public opinion toward the conflict has soured, more so since Ukraine has intensified its attacks on energy and logistics infrastructure inside Russia.

The non-governmental Levada Center — which is on the Kremlin's "foreign agents" list — charts support at around 66%, the lowest since Russia launched its attack against neighboring Ukraine on February 24, 2022.

The Kremlin has cracked down on opposition to the war with strict censorship rules and mass arrests, with many activists and journalists preferring to flee than to face potentially deadly persecution by staying in Russia.

Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah

World.title: Colombia earthquake: Death toll rises to over 100
World.content:
A powerful earthquake, measured at magnitude 7.4, has struck Colombia, killing dozens of people and trapping many under rubble. Cities including Cali, Pereira and Manizales were among the hardest-hit.

A powerful earthquake shook western Colombia early on Monday morning.

Around six hours after the quake struck, Colombia's president said that 111 people had been confirmed dead around the country.

Rescue teams were working to free residents after buildings collapsed in Cali and other cities.

The epicenter was on the eastern tip of the Choco province on Colombia's Pacific coast.

The government has declared a state of emergency.

What is the latest?

Colombia's newly-inaugurated President Abelardo de la Espriella said that he had personally taken charge of the government's response to the emergency.

He said that locating anyone still potentially trapped was the highest priority for rescuers and declared a national state of emergency.

"As of 12:30 [local time], the toll stood at 111 dead and 87 injured, with 1,575 homes damaged, 37 completely destroyed, 61 buildings collapsed, and 18 health centers and 52 schools damaged," de la Espriella said from Bogota.

More than 100 dead in Colombia after major earthquake To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the EU stands "ready to provide more support" to Colombia. The bloc's satellite service, Copernicus, has already been mobilized to aid rescuers.

"Tonight, Europe's heart is with the people of Colombia," she wrote on social media.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US was "closely monitoring" the situation and stood "ready to support the people of Colombia."

What's happening on the ground?

The mayor of Cali, Alejandro Eder, said that at least 20 buildings had collapsed, in some cases with people trapped inside.

"Residents of Cali, we currently have at least 20 collapsed structures in the city with people trapped inside; we are already managing this emergency alongside all of Cali's rescue agencies," Eder said on Instagram, posting an accompanying video statement. "I have requested support — specifically rescue personnel — from the mayors of Bogota and Medellin."

Authorities in the Valle del Cauca, whose capital city is Cali, said that at least 27 people had died in the quake, in numbers issued prior to the president's address.

Officials in Risaralda had said that 40 people had died across the state, at least 18 of them in the capital Pereira based on earlier comments from the mayor.

The governor of the Choco region where the quake's epicenter was located, Nubia Carolina Cordoba-Curi, said there were 12 dead and 84 wounded in her district as of lunch time local time.

And the mayor of Manizales, Jorge Eduardo Rojas, said in a radio interview that two people were killed in his city, in the Caldas region not far northeast of Pereira.

Residents in Cali tried to rush to safety in the aftermath of Monday's earthquake Image: Santiago Saldarriaga/AP Photo/picture alliance

Colombia's civil aviation authority reported damage at six relatively minor airports and said flights were suspended while it was examined.

"Damage is reported at the airports of Pereira, Manizales, Quibdo, Armenia, Cartago, and Buenaventura. For safety reasons, air operations at these terminals remain suspended until structural damage to the infrastructure is assessed," it wrote online, later adding Cali's airport to this list.

What do we know about the quake's size and location?

The US Geological Survey (USGS) measured the quake at magnitude 7.4. Colombia's national authority at first logged a smaller figure but later revised its reading up to 7.4 as well.

The epicenter was located just south of the Tatama National Nature Reserve, near Choco's eastern state border.

One of the towers at the Cathedral of Manizales was damaged by the quake Image: John Jairo Bonilla/AP Photo/picture alliance

The epicenter was roughly equidistant from Colombia's three main cities, Bogota to its east, Medellin to its north and Cali to its south.

The closest major population center, Cartago, is home to about 140,000 people and around 30 kilometers (roughly 20 miles) from the quake's epicenter.

The USGS said the quake was also quite deep, striking around 107 kilometers below the ground. It estimated that most of the western half of Colombia would feel the tremors .

Tremors could also be felt in neighboring Ecuador to the south, and to the north and east in Panama and Venezuela.

USGS also recorded a fairly large aftershock, at magnitude 5.0, a little under an hour after the main quake.

The so-called Ring of Fire — the world's most active belt of tectonic plates and volcanoes encircling the Pacific Ocean — runs along Colombia's coastline not far from the epicenter of Monday's quake.

Edited by: Rebecca Staudenmaier
