World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018861/Video Game Accounts Can Be Inherited, Chinese Court Rules
World.title: Video Game Accounts Can Be Inherited, Chinese Court Rules
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018861/Video Game Accounts Can Be Inherited, Chinese Court Rules
World.content:
A Beijing court has ruled in favor of a mother seeking to inherit her late son’s 87 online gaming accounts, selecting the dispute as an example case to provide judges with legal direction on similar future proceedings involving digital assets.

The case, reported Monday by the People’s Court Daily, a newspaper affiliated with China’s Supreme People’s Court, involved the inheritance rights to the accounts of an avid gamer surnamed Gu, who passed away last year at 36 due to oral cancer.

With China’s internet penetration rate reaching 80.1% by the end of 2025, the case comes as the country faces increasing pressure to handle the growing volume of digital assets left behind by deceased users.

Since China’s Civil Code — which states that digital assets are protected by law — took effect in 2021, courts have increasingly recognized the property value of digital assets. In 2025, the Supreme People’s Court created a separate case category for disputes involving data and online virtual property.

Between 2010 and 2021, Gu registered accounts on games by Chinese game developer Changyou, acquiring valuable in-game assets due to having “built up the accounts” over the years, according to the report.

After Gu’s passing, his mother, surnamed Chen, asked the company to transfer the accounts into her name so she could sell them to help cover her living expenses, as she relied on a low income and no family support.

The company denied her request, however, citing their user agreement, which states that it retains ownership of all account-related data, including account information, game characters, virtual items, and in-game currency.

Chen then sued the company. In April, the Beijing Shijingshan District People’s Court ruled that although ownership of the accounts rested with the company, the accounts had independent economic value because Gu had invested time, effort, and money in them. As a result, the court found that the right of use of the accounts, though not their ownership, could be inherited.

The court ordered the company to complete the transfer of the accounts’ real-name registration to Chen within 15 days after the ruling took effect. Chen is the sole legal heir to the accounts, as Gu’s daughter waived her inheritance rights.

Many online platforms prohibit account transfers or inheritance. But platforms’ user agreements cannot override a user’s legal inheritance rights, Zhang Yingzhou, the judge presiding over the case, told local media.

“Heirs inherit the economic interests attached to the right to use an account, not ownership of the account itself,” the judge said.

Other incidents related to the transfer of digital assets have made headlines in China recently, including a case related to the recycling of popular Chinese-American singer Coco Lee’s phone number by her telecom operator after she committed suicide in 2023.

In 2025, a user who registered for domestic music streaming platform NetEase with a newly purchased mobile phone number was inadvertently logged into Lee’s verified artist account. NetEase explained that the phone number originally linked to Lee’s account had been reassigned to a new user without unbinding the account link to NetEase. The incident sparked widespread discussion on domestic social media about digital privacy, account security, and the management of digital assets after death.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018856/The Chinese Factory Town Betting on America’s Mahjong Boom
World.title: The Chinese Factory Town Betting on America’s Mahjong Boom
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018856/The Chinese Factory Town Betting on America’s Mahjong Boom
World.content:
JIANGSU, East China — “We are looking for a factory that can produce acrylic mahjong tiles.”

Hua Fangyi repeated that pitch at nearly 30 factories in Taixing, a city in eastern China’s Jiangsu province known for manufacturing mahjong tiles. “Almost every factory refused,” she says.

After quitting her job to start an export business last October, Hua, 28, spotted a surge in overseas demand for American mahjong. Believing the opportunity might last only a few months, she planned to test the market with just a few dozen sets.

But Taixing’s factories were built for large runs of traditional Chinese mahjong, not the small batches of brightly colored acrylic tiles overseas buyers wanted. Some produced only conventional melamine sets; others required minimum orders far beyond what Hua could afford.

Then Hua found a factory with 20 American mahjong sets in stock. She bought the entire batch, and it sold out almost immediately.

Within months, she had built a company shipping more than 5,000 sets a month and generating roughly $400,000 in monthly sales. Across Taixing, factories that had once turned away from American mahjong were now chasing the same overseas buyers.

“Almost every factory is now making American mahjong,” Hua says.

The shift came as rising material costs and intensifying competition squeezed margins on traditional sets. Overseas demand offered higher returns, prompting established factories to buy equipment, hire workers, and adapt their production lines to the elaborate designs sought by American buyers.

The opportunity has also drawn a new generation of entrepreneurs to Taixing: former tech workers, salespeople, and export traders hoping to manufacture the tiles and build brands of their own.

Together, they are all betting on a boom whose limits remain unclear. For now, overseas orders have given Taixing’s mahjong industry fresh momentum, sending an old manufacturing center racing to master a game it barely recognized a year ago.

Follow the dots

Growing up around her family’s garment factory and later working in international e-commerce at Alibaba, Hua had experience with both manufacturing and overseas sales. She began searching for products that could find a market abroad.

She continued using the habits she developed in product operations, tracking trends on social media platforms such as Instagram and Facebook and monitoring sales performance on overseas independent websites. American mahjong stood out.

The game itself, however, has a long history in the U.S. The governing body for American mahjong, the National Mah Jongg League, was founded in 1937 with 32 members; it now has more than 350,000 members and publishes a new card of official hands and rules each year.

More recently, American brands such as Oh My Mahjong have helped recast mahjong tiles as colorful, premium lifestyle products, while influencers and social clubs have brought the game to younger players seeking in-person connection.

In April 2026, review platform Yelp reported that U.S. searches for mahjong clubs had jumped 4,467% between September 2024 and August 2025, compared with the previous 12 months. Oh My Mahjong’s sets now sell for $350 to $475, with most priced around $400 — versus the roughly 100 yuan ($15) many Chinese sets sell for in China on e-commerce platform Taobao.

But Hua initially expected the opportunity to be short-lived. Without historical data on American mahjong, she looked to previous domestic product cycles, which often peaked around specific festivals. She expected demand to surge around Christmas, just two months after she first spotted the trend.

Moving quickly to find a supplier, Hua and her father, who runs the family’s garment factory, drove several hundred kilometers from Ningbo, in neighboring Zhejiang province, to Taixing.

But many workshops had no obvious signs and appeared on maps only under broad categories such as “entertainment products.” From the road, little revealed what was being made inside.

Hua struggled to understand the local dialect, so her father asked residents and security guards where they could find factory owners. “We’d only know we’d found the right place after spotting a set or two of mahjong tiles,” she says. “They’d point us to a building and a floor, and we’d keep looking until we found the boss.”

The industry was all around them. A search for “mahjong” on Qichacha, a Chinese corporate database, returns nearly 180 businesses in Taixing, many of them small workshops specializing in a single stage of production.

The cluster grew from a household trade dating to the 1980s, when local families cut and polished tiles by hand from bamboo and ox bone. Over time, production split among specialized workshops handling tile blanks, engraving, polishing, printing, and packaging.

“If one family made money from it, the neighbors would learn too,” says Zhu Ronggen, whose father was among Taixing’s earliest mahjong makers. “One person taught another, and slowly the whole village started making mahjong.”

Zhu grew up inside that manufacturing network. After studying mechanical engineering, he returned to Taixing in 2015 and opened his own factory. By the following year, he was producing traditional sets for China’s domestic market.

So when a customer first asked him to make an American set, Zhu, now 48, assumed it would be a minor variation on a familiar product.

“Chinese mahjong designs have barely changed for decades,” Zhu says. “American mahjong is completely different. A circle tile could be a football or a bunch of grapes. One grape stands for one dot, and nine grapes represent nine dots.”

American sets also include Arabic numerals and joker tiles, while familiar symbols are constantly reworked around seasonal themes and customers’ ideas. Summer collections feature seashells and aquatic plants; Christmas designs use Santa hats and trees.

And while traditional Chinese sets are usually molded from melamine in a narrow range of colors, American buyers prefer acrylic tiles with richer palettes, sometimes built from six or seven colored layers visible along the edge.

“Every customer wants their own concept,” Zhu says. “The color palettes are also much richer than those used in China.”

Chinese players, he says, tend to value weight, legibility, and how the tiles feel in the hand. American buyers, by contrast, want sets distinctive enough to display and expressive enough to reflect their tastes.

“I gradually understood that they weren’t just buying mahjong to play mahjong,” Zhu says. “A lot of the time, they’re buying a lifestyle.”

Factory reset

Inside Zhu’s factory, traditional Chinese mahjong and its American reinvention sit side by side. Dust-covered melamine slabs are stacked near the entrance, while baskets of brightly colored acrylic tiles and export cartons crowd the corridors beyond.

By 4 p.m., Zhu is usually outside the workshop, surrounded by cardboard boxes as he seals packages and confirms overseas delivery addresses with couriers. He moves between the packing area and loading site until sunset.

After the workers leave, he returns to his office to answer inquiries that accumulated during the afternoon. His wife stays at the UV printer, often working until midnight.

At 7 a.m. the next day, Zhu unlocks the factory gate and starts again.

For years, inquiries from new buyers came weeks or even months apart. Orders from Zhu’s long-term domestic clients remained steady, but rising material costs and intensifying competition had squeezed profits. To keep costs down, he and his wife took on work once handled by employees.

Now, he receives dozens of inquiries every day — from foreign trade companies, Amazon sellers, independent online retailers, and buyers on Alibaba.

“I used to make just 20 sets of American mahjong a year,” he says. “Now, I can turn out 200 sets a day.”

Unlike traditional Chinese sets, which can be reproduced using fixed molds, each American order requires new adjustments to engraving, printing, and coloring. A batch of 300 to 400 acrylic sets takes 15 to 20 days to complete — three to five days longer than the same number of Chinese sets.

“People buy them the way they buy clothes,” Zhu says. “What’s fashionable this year may be completely different next year.”

To keep up, Zhu has invested another 1 million yuan ($148,000) in laser engravers, UV printers, and other equipment. But he has hired only two or three additional workers, leaving his family to absorb much of the extra labor.

At the center of the workshop, a giant white sack hangs above a mound of acrylic tiles. Zhu’s parents, both in their 80s, sit on opposite sides of the pile, lifting the pieces one by one and arranging them into neat rows, every face turned in the same direction. Their hands move with a steady, practiced rhythm.

They work from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m., the same hours as the factory’s other employees.

“I can do 100 sets a day,” Zhu’s father says. “Workers’ wages aren’t cheap. At least the two of us can save a few hundred yuan.”

A few steps away, Jin Guihua, 62, sorts black tiles before they are colored. Their engraved patterns are barely visible against the dark surface, so she lifts each rack toward the window, tilting it until the light catches the shallow lines.

She scans the rows for matching designs, tapping each selected tile against the edge of the table before setting it aside. Sometimes she checks more than five tiles before finding the next match.

Jin once sorted about 150 sets a day. The smaller tiles and changing patterns of American mahjong have reduced her output to about 60.

“The designs are more complicated and harder to identify,” she says.

Brand new

This past March, five young entrepreneurs arrived in Taixing to start a mahjong business.

A few minutes from Zhu’s family-run factory, they turned a village house into a workshop. Machines occupied the ground floor; their bedrooms were upstairs. There were no fixed hours or weekends.

Between them, the five had experience in sales, technology, and international trade. None had ever made a mahjong tile.



Li Mingzhi, 30, leads the venture, which operates under the name SenJoy Mahjong. A former Alibaba employee, he saw American mahjong as a chance to sell a higher-value product overseas. He recruited his former colleague Wang Hao, his younger brother, and several childhood friends from northwestern China’s Gansu province to build the venture.

“I never imagined I’d move to such a remote village to start a business,” says Wang, 28.

Zhu estimates that nearly 30 new factories have sprung up in Taixing over the past year as entrepreneurs rush into American mahjong. The town’s fragmented supply chain has allowed outsiders to enter without building a factory from scratch.

“Here, you don’t need to build an entire production line yourself,” Li tells Sixth Tone. “You can outsource each step and focus on design and branding.”

In practice, however, the workshop became a crash course in manufacturing.

“Every day is unpredictable,” Li says. “Customers can call at any time, and problems can emerge at every stage — production, design, communication, quality inspection. Working until 3 or 4 a.m. is normal.”

The new equipment offered precision but no ready-made solution for mahjong production: sizes varied, hand-cut pieces did not match machine-cut ones, and every fault required another round of testing.

“Almost every step brought a different problem,” Wang says.

The UV printer proved especially difficult. Each design had to be aligned by hand, and a shift of just 1 millimeter could push the ink outside the engraved lines.

The night before Sixth Tone’s visit, all five stayed up until 3 a.m. trying to solve the problem. “Before entering the industry, I thought making mahjong would be simple,” says Wang. “Once I started, I realized American sets are closer to handicrafts.”

Despite the setbacks, the team produced and sold about 1,000 sets in its first few months, generating roughly 230,000 yuan in sales. Its customers included businesses selling on Amazon.

Li put 1.5 million yuan of his own savings into the venture. “Based on our current orders,” says Li, “we expect the business to recover that investment within six months.”

To avoid becoming another contract manufacturer in Taixing’s crowded supply chain, the team began working with outside designers to develop original sets. It also launched an independent website and overseas social media accounts.

“For us, building a brand starts with original design,” Li says. “We might become the first company in Taixing — and perhaps one of the first in China — to build a real mahjong brand instead of simply manufacturing for others.”

The team hopes to reach buyers directly through social media, influencers, online sellers, and brick-and-mortar retailers.

Their bestseller uses a coral-reef theme. Against a shimmering blue base, coral motifs represent bamboo tiles, shells stand in for circles, and small fish serve as jokers.

“As long as the designs aren’t ugly, we’re not worried about sales,” Li says. “Right now, demand far exceeds supply.”

Wang is more cautious. Today’s buyers, he says, remain a relatively small group with strong spending power. If American mahjong reaches a broader market, more manufacturers will follow, he says, adding: “Price wars are unavoidable.”

Hua, one of the first Chinese traders to bet on American mahjong, has watched competitors multiply within months.

When she launched the business, Hua handled every part of the operation herself, often staying up late to respond to customers in the U.S. and sleeping as little as two hours a night. Today, her Ningbo-based company employs about 10 people and provides customer service around the clock.

But the market that once seemed wide open has become more crowded. Designs that once sold out quickly are now easier to source, and more suppliers are competing for the same orders.

“The conversion rate isn’t as good as before,” Hua says. Her sales data show that fewer visitors become inquiries, and fewer inquiries turn into confirmed orders.

“The profit margins were much higher in the beginning, but now they have dropped significantly,” she says. “I think this is probably an inevitable stage for any viral product.”

She, too, has started developing designs of her own.

Last month, she began experimenting with AI to create early concepts before working with freelance designers to refine them. Her first ideas included themes inspired by witches, tennis, flowers, and Christmas.

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: Workers sort uncarved and unpainted mahjong tiles at Zhu Ronggen’s factory in Taixing, Jiangsu province, June 2026. Wu Huiyuan/Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018855/Chinese Rafting Park in Hot Water Over ‘Female Companion’ Service
World.title: Chinese Rafting Park in Hot Water Over ‘Female Companion’ Service
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018855/Chinese Rafting Park in Hot Water Over ‘Female Companion’ Service
World.content:
A river rafting tourist attraction in southwestern China has come under fire for offering “temporary girlfriends” and “very attractive” female companions who hold hands with, hug, and kiss customers while they raft.

Reported widely last week, the female companion service was offered by Luobei River Drifting, a popular rafting attraction in Guizhou province, beginning this summer. The rafting route, known for its thrilling rapids, lasts between 1.5 and 4 hours and covers up to 12.5 kilometers. Tickets cost up to 238 yuan ($35) per person.

In recent years, rafting attractions around China, including in the central Henan province, the eastern Jiangsu province, and the southern Hainan province, have launched scripted “NPC” rafting experiences, hiring workers to act as wolves, monkeys, bears, and frogs, as well as characters from the classic novel “Journey to the West” while customers raft. Related videos on Chinese social media have garnered tens of thousands of likes.

An undercover reporter at High Wind News, a platform under state-run media outlet Chinese Business View, posing as a customer contacted the attraction’s customer service on the messaging app WeChat, which informed them that they could choose from three service packages: a 398-yuan “highly attractive” companion who accompanies the rider with no additional physical contact, a 1,288-yuan partner with “upgraded appearance with polite physical contact,” and a 1,988-yuan “temporary girlfriend” option.

Customer service sent the reporter several photos — purported to be real pictures of the female companions — along with profiles of more than 30 women, including their height, weight, and age. Some photos were labeled “pure green,” indicating the companion’s service does not include “sexual behavior or contact.”

“The 1,988-yuan package is just like dating — you can hold hands, hug, and kiss,” the staff member told the undercover reporter, hinting that there could be further meetups after the initial rafting encounter.

“We create a legitimate setting for you to meet and communicate. We’re essentially just the intermediary,” the customer service representative added, claiming to receive around 400 groups of customers a day. The staff member also said the rafting park had more than 1,000 workers and required companions to be reserved in advance.

An account on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, by the name of “Luobei River NPC Scripted Drifting” had reportedly posted promotional videos of young women accompanying tourists during rafting and water activities, with slogans such as, “What heals you isn’t the scenery, but the emotional value.” The account has since been deleted.

Employees at the tourist attraction later confirmed to domestic media that companion services were available and directed reporters to the same customer service WeChat account.

In an official announcement posted on WeChat last Thursday, however, the company behind the park denied any connection to the female companion service, saying a separate company had privately launched the service.

A day later, on July 31, the local tourism bureau announced that Luobei River Drifting had agreed to collaborate with a management company specializing in upgraded rafting experiences, where tourists become the protagonists in stories instead of passive sightseers. According to the company’s official WeChat account, it had signed the cooperation agreement on May 6.

On July 31, the rafting operator was ordered by the local government to suspend operations for “rectification.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Female rafting companions. From Xiaohongshu)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018854/Check in, Log on, Stay for Months: Life at China’s 9-Cent Internet Café
World.title: Check in, Log on, Stay for Months: Life at China’s 9-Cent Internet Café
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018854/Check in, Log on, Stay for Months: Life at China’s 9-Cent Internet Café
World.content:
Outside an unassuming three-story building in downtown Kangyi Town, in the eastern Shandong province, hangs a sign that reads: “Striving to be the cheapest internet café in China.”

With charges as low as 0.6 yuan ($0.09) an hour, it’s certainly not false advertising. Yet step inside and you will find not just gamers chasing rock-bottom prices, but also a mix of locals and out-of-towners with myriad tales of misfortune, many looking to rise from their own rock bottom.

Here, customers can bathe and do laundry for free, enjoy a lunch of meat and vegetables for just 10 yuan, and even sleep in reclining esports chairs. For those looking to get back on their feet, it’s the ultimate low-to-no-cost option.

Like many of its patrons, the café’s owner, Wang Zhongkai, is also just trying to survive. After struggling to keep the doors open for more than a decade, the 38-year-old decided to slash his prices last year to attract more foot traffic.

The move certainly accomplished that — although it’s also inadvertently created a shelter for people in hard times.

After seeing a video about the internet café on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, Wang’s first out-of-town customer traveled 800 kilometers from neighboring Jiangsu province to “seek refuge” — and ended up staying for eight months.

Changing fortunes

China had roughly 122,600 licensed internet cafés last year, up 12% from 2024, according to the Internet Access Service Association of China. However, data from the Ministry of Culture and Tourism shows that average annual revenue fell from 216,000 yuan to 197,000 yuan over that same period.

Hardware is the biggest investment. With ever-changing technology, a new computer costing 15,000 yuan can lose a third of its value within a year, with software requiring constant paid-for upgrades.

Wang’s is one of only two surviving internet cafés in Kangyi. The business today has more than 150 computers of various specs, including 35 priced at 0.6 yuan an hour. The other machines in the main hall range from 0.9 yuan to 3 yuan an hour, while private one-person rooms are available for 99 yuan a day.

From nearly empty every day, Wang has seen occupancy increase to about 90%. At nighttime, the second floor is illuminated by the shifting colors of the PC screens, with the faces of customers — almost entirely men — aglow with yellow, green, red, and blue hues. Some are fast asleep, wrapped in summer blankets, headphones dangling from their neck.

Over the years, Wang, a father of three, has tried many ways to increase his income. He tried opening a grocery store on the side, which saw him lose 500,000 yuan in about six months. To recover, in 2023, he moved to Beijing — leaving his wife in charge of the café — to become a daijia, a designated driver for hire, working 15 hours a day. One day, he was so exhausted that he fell asleep while riding his electric bike and crashed.

He knows all too well that sometimes people just need to get through a rough patch. While living in the capital, he would pay 15 yuan to spend the night at an internet café where he could charge his e-bike and get hot water.

Wang returned to Kangyi in 2025. Today he helps his customers find low-cost rooms in town for as little as 200 yuan a month, with no deposit. For those who can’t even afford that, he lets them sleep for free in the café’s luxurious esports chairs.

He also advertises day-labor gigs available nearby, such as sorting packages at a courier depot or casual shifts at a machinery plant. Most of his customers decline, however, either because they’re not fit enough to handle manual labor or can’t stomach the idea of being bossed around.

His wife and mother-in-law are responsible for preparing lunch every day at the café, with one meat dish, one vegetable dish, and mountains of rice and steamed buns. Most diners pay 10 yuan, but those without a penny eat for free.

The showers and an industrial-size washing machine are also free to use — Wang even provides soap and detergent.

Despite the increased foot traffic, Wang’s profit margins remain wafer-thin. He says his family has invested more than 700,000 yuan in new computers, yet their revenue streams comprise only the cut-rate internet fees, sales of food and drink, and the occasional livestream on Douyin, during which some viewers will send virtual gifts. Except for relatives, the business has only one employee — an elderly male cleaner.

Boosting opportunities

Qiang Yu, a 30-something from Huaibei in the eastern Anhui province, has spent every day and night in the “0.6-yuan zone” for nearly a year. Like many others here, he makes money as a “game booster,” which involves playing video games to level up someone else’s account. His specialty is the online role-playing game Legend of Mir 2.

High-level accounts in popular games are worth tens of thousands of yuan, and cheating can lead to a permanent ban by game developers. Account owners are usually unwilling to hand their username and password to strangers, but Wang has built a reputation among several clients, offering a personal guarantee for any losses. He regularly farms out orders to the boosters at his internet café — and doesn’t even take a cut.

In the past, Qiang did manual jobs — digging gravel by the railway tracks, getting paid by the meter, his hands raw and blistered at the end of a shift, as well as toiling at factories making garments, lights, and electronics. It left him with a “crushing depression,” he says.

Qiang now earns just over 100 yuan for 12 hours’ work and survives on just 25 yuan a day. If, in a year, he has 10,000 yuan in his pocket, he plans to go home and clear the weeds that have taken over his courtyard.

Cao Ti Lie, a gamer who asked to be identified only by his username, arrived in Kangyi from Foshan, in the southern Guangdong province, in June. He grew up in video arcades, and now regularly livestreams to 60,000 subscribers on Douyin as he competes in the classic King of Fighters ’97.

Gaming used to be fun, he says; now it’s a full-time job. “The heart of the boy I was is dead. When you have to face life, it gets erased.”

The 41-year-old previously ran a business in Foshan and was making 30,000 yuan a month, but bad investments and a gambling habit saw his debts pile up. His wife left with their children, and then his mother suffered a stroke and broke her hip, losing the ability to care for herself.

Soon after spotting a video about Wang’s internet café, he hopped on a train here. His only goal is to save enough money to cover the costs of his mother’s nursing home.

Future is now

Wang’s day starts at 8 a.m. He scrubs five toilets, restocks the fridge, wipes down the keyboards, picks up any trash from the night before, and then takes his spot at the front counter.

He sees plenty of local faces come and go, but many of the out-of-towners are now permanent fixtures. In February, the café hosted about 40 people on Chinese New Year’s Eve, an important day on the calendar for family reunion.

Mao Lifen, a gamer from the northern Shanxi province who arrived in May, says he tries not to think about the future. He used to have a plan — work at a factory for five years, save up, and open a fruit shop. This was derailed when he and his colleagues had a falling out with the factory management and quit.

He went to work in food delivery and partnered with a friend to open a restaurant, maxing out several credit cards to the tune of 100,000 yuan and losing it all. Mao then tried starting a business with another friend, who ran off with all their money. A string of bad investments appears to have killed his interest in making plans.

His only thought now is to get through this year. “I’ve got food and drink — what is there to be unhappy about?” he says. At Wang’s internet café, he takes boosting orders for the first-person tactical shooter game Delta Force. When he’s not playing, he likes to walk up to the rooftop to look at the trees in the distance.

Mao likes this life that requires next to no human contact: everyone stares at their screen, submerged in the game. With his headphones on, there is no “outside world.”

This year, a wannabe entrepreneur from out of town visited Wang with a view to copying his business model elsewhere. Wang laid it out for him: 150 computers plus renovations, licensing, and other expenses mean at least 2 million yuan upfront; profits will unlikely keep pace with the equipment’s depreciation; and a minimum of three or four employees are needed to run 24/7. The visitor listened patiently and immediately abandoned the plan.

Wang knows he’s too deep into the industry to pull out. When he was young, he dreamed of making a fortune and owning a luxury car, but now “I know my limits,” he says. With a 30-year mortgage and still owing 110,000 yuan for equipment, his only wish is to draw customers and stay afloat.

(For privacy reasons, Qiang Yu and Mao Lifen are pseudonyms.)

Reported by Jiang Wanru.

A version of this article originally appeared in White Night Workshop. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: Kiong Xin Xi; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

(Header image: Customers sleep in the esports chairs, at Wang’s internet café in Kangyi Town, June 2026. Jiang Wanru/White Night Workshop)

World.content:
WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW

The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.

On this page, we bring you the latest updates, analyses, videos, and photos as the trial of the Vice President unfolds.

World.title: DPWH seeks P107.4 billion for flood control projects in 2027
World.content:
Acting Budget Secretary Kim de Leon says that this is meant to support ongoing flood control projects

MANILA, Philippines – The Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) is seeking P107.4 billion for flood control projects for 2027, a year after the government scrapped funding for such projects amid a corruption scandal.

Acting Budget Secretary Kim de Leon explained in a press briefing on Tuesday, August 11, that the funds are meant to support ongoing flood control projects.

“Hindi naman po natin puwedeng pabayaan ‘yung mga naumpisahan nang flood control projects. Mas hindi po magiging maayos ang epekto kung mananatiling nakatiwangwang ‘yung mga naumpisahan nang flood control projects,” De Leon said.

(We cannot neglect the flood control projects that are already underway. Abandoning these ongoing flood control projects will only lead to far worse consequences.)

De Leon also pointed out that flood control projects require spending beyond their initial construction costs, as some facilities come with recurring operating expenses. He cited pumping stations, which need to be maintained and operated every year.

During the previous budget deliberations, the DPWH scrapped P252 billion worth of locally funded flood control projects from the 2026 National Expenditure Program (NEP), following President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s directive.

The decision came after the government uncovered substandard and ghost flood control projects across the country. Some government officials — including senators, congressmen, and DPWH personnel — allegedly benefited from these projects.

Under the Marcos administration, the funding for flood control projects spiked.

To prevent the recurrence of ghost projects, De Leon said the DPWH has ensured that projects included in the NEP are properly tagged, with identified locations and corresponding programs of work.

The DPWH got the second biggest allocation of P644 billion under the proposed 2027 budget. The allocation for the flood control project accounts for 16% of the agency’s total proposed allocation.

Aside from the DPWH allocation, the Metropolitan Manila Development Authority is seeking P3.41 billion for its flood control program, including the operation of flood control structures. – Rappler.com

World.title: Rappler’s 2026 Board of Directors
World.content:
Former Microsoft CEO in the Philippines Peter Maquera is the new member of the Board

MANILA, Philippines – Former CEO of Microsoft Philippines Peter Maquera and veteran capital markets practitioner Gus Cosio are the latest members of the Board of Directors of Rappler, Inc.

Maquera joined the Rappler Board in July 2026, while Cosio became Board director in 2022. They joined the six existing members of the Rappler Board: Maria Ressa, Glenda Gloria, Manny Ayala, Winnie Monsod, Tony La Viña, and Federico Prieto.

In their meeting on July 3, 2026, the Board reelected Ressa as Board president and Gloria as chairperson.

Here are their brief profiles:

Manny Ayala, Director

Manny is a founder at Hatchd Inc, a technology incubator focused on building great Internet and mobile brands, and currently the global managing director of Endeavor Philippines. He was previously a managing director at IRG Ltd, a HK-based M&A boutique focused on the telecoms, media and tech industries. At IRG, Manny focused on a variety of projects in the Internet, mobile, television and online gaming sectors.

Manny was the number two executive at Discovery Networks Asia, instrumental in building Discovery Channel and Animal Planet into top-rated TV channels across the region. Prior to this, he served as deputy general manager for TNT and Cartoon Network Asia, an AOL Time Warner TV channel, where he was a key member of the team that launched the service across the Asia Pacific. Prior to that, Manny worked for STAR TV where he was part of the team that acquired the Don Bluth Animation Studio as well as a number of the world’s key Chinese-language film libraries. Manny has an MBA from the Harvard Graduate School of Business and a BA, cum laude, from Yale University.

Augusto “Gus” M. Cosio, Jr., Director

Gus retired as president of First Metro Asset Management Inc., a Metrobank subsidiary in June 2018 after joining the First Metro Investment Corporation Investment group in 2006 where he had been an active member of its investment committee.

His experience in investments and the capital markets span both local and international institutions. Gus had been an international capital markets practitioner for many years having been worked with Banque Nationale de Paris and Banque Paribas the predecessors of the present BNP Paribas prior to their merger. He worked in Hong Kong and Singapore for the Paribas capital markets group and in the Manila Off-shore Branch of Banque Nationale de Paris. He had been president of PNB Securities Inc. and a member of the board of the Philippine Stock Exchange. He also served as Senior Vice President of Security Bank Corporation and SB Capital Inc. Gus remains active in post retirement activities holding management positions and directorships in a few enterprises.

Glenda Gloria, Chairperson

Glenda co-founded Rappler in July 2011 and is currently its executive editor.

She has worked for the Philippine Daily Inquirer, The Manila Times, the Philippine Center for Investigative Journalism, and for international news agencies. She co-founded the Philippines’ top investigative magazine Newsbreak, which started as a newsweekly and later merged with Rappler. From 2008 to January 2011, she managed ANC, the ABS-CBN News Channel, as its chief operating officer.

Glenda has written books on the military, conflict, and politics, among them the award-winning Under the Crescent Moon: Rebellion in Mindanao (with Marites Dañguilan Vitug). A British Chevening scholar, she holds a master’s degree in political sociology from the London School of Economics and Political Science. In May 2018, Glenda finished her Nieman journalism fellowship at Harvard University.

Antonio “Tony” La Viña, Director

Dean Antonio Gabriel La Viña is Associate Director of Manila Observatory where he heads the Klima Center and a professor of law, philosophy, politics and governance in several universities. He is the managing partner of La Viña Zarate and Associates, a development and social change progressive law firm and a member of the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague: He is founding president of the Movement Against Disinformation Tony also writes for Rappler’s Thought Leaders section.

Peter Maquera, Director

Peter is former CEO of Microsoft Philippines, where he led the company’s efforts in cloud, AI, and cybersecurity. Earlier, Peter spent a significant portion of his career with the Ayala Group, notably as senior vice president of Globe Telecom’s Enterprise Group, president of Globe Telecom International Business Holdings, and deputy CEO of LiveIt Investments, Ltd., Ayala Corporation’s holding company for the BPO sector. Across his career his work centered on scaling complex ICT operations within the Philippines and across international markets.

Peter is a trustee of the Makati Business Club chairing the Philippine-US Business Council, and a trustee of the American Chamber of Commerce, co-chairing the ICT committee. Peter is also a member of the Private Sector Advisory Council (Digital Pillar), and a Board Advisor to the Asian Institute of Management RSN Center for Competitiveness. Peter earned his undergraduate degree in Engineering and a master’s in business administration from the University of Southern California.

Winnie Monsod, Director

An economist, teacher, writer and broadcaster, Winnie was appointed the Philippines’ first socio-economic planning secretary after the fall of the Marcos dictatorship in 1986. She is professor emerita at the University of the Philippines’ (UP) School of Economics, where she taught starting 1983.

Winnie served at the United Nations Committee on Development Policy and was convenor and member of the Advisory Board of the UNDP Human Development Report. For 11 years, she was chairperson of the Philippine Human Development Network. She also served on the advisory board of the South Centre in Geneva and the Board of Trustees of the International Food Policy Research Institute based in Washington, DC, and was a member of the High Level Task Force of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights. Winnie finished her degree in economics in UP and obtained her masters in economics at the University of Pennsylvania.

Federico “Fred” Prieto, Director

Fred is a lawyer with litigation and corporate practice. For his litigation practice he handles criminal, civil, labor and tax cases. His corporate practice involves mergers and acquisitions, business organization and restructuring, IPO offering and regulatory compliance, among others. He is a 2006 graduate of San Beda University’s College of Law in Mendiola and was admitted to the Bar in May 2007.

Maria Ressa, President

Maria is co-founder and CEO of Rappler. In October 2021, she was one of two journalists awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in recognition of her “efforts to safeguard freedom of expression, which is a precondition for democracy and lasting peace.” In 2022, she was appointed by the United Nations Secretary-General to the Leadership Panel of the Internet Governance Forum and serves as its Vice-Chair. In March 2026, she was selected by the United Nations to sit on the Independent International Scientific Panel on AI and serves as its Co-Chair.

She is a also a professor of practice at Columbia University’s School of International and Public Affairs. Maria authored Seeds of Terror: An Eyewitness Account of Al-Qaeda’s Newest Center of Operations in Southeast Asia and From Bin Laden to Facebook. Her most recent book, How to Stand Up to a Dictator, has been translated into more than 25 languages. – Rappler.com

World.title: This Puerto Princesa community rethinks plastic waste, builds a classroom out of it
World.content:
BAYANIHAN. Students, volunteers, and community members gather to prepare materials for Bahay Pangarap, working together through hands-on construction.

About 45 minutes from Puerto Princesa City proper, a small off-grid community in Barangay Bacungan is proving that sustainability begins with people

PALAWAN, Philippines – Beyond Puerto Princesa City’s bustling streets, a narrow road winds toward an off-grid community in Barangay Bacungan, where pristine beaches, forests, and a slower way of life surround Maia Earth Village, home to the Maia Earth Organization Incorporated founded in 2010.

About 15 minutes from the village stands Bahay Pangarap at Bacungan National High School (BNHS), a mud wall classroom built not only with earth from the community but also with more than 2,000 discarded plastic bottles transformed into ecobricks.

The project was made possible through the collaboration of Maia, Malaya Permakultura, and the Department of Education.

Bayanihan spirit

What began as an environmental initiative grew into a community-wide effort that brought together students, teachers, volunteers, and residents through the Filipino spirit of bayanihan.

Over two years, from 2023 to 2025, students collected plastic bottles, filled them tightly with nonbiodegradable waste to create ecobricks, and helped construct what Maia describes as the country’s first student-built mud wall classroom. It was completed in July 2025.

FEET AT WORK. Volunteers and students work together to mix the materials needed for the construction, making the building process a shared learning experience. Photo courtesy of Maia Earth Organization Inc.

For Pi Villaraza, founder of Maia Earth Organization Incorporated, Bacungan offered more than just a location for the project.

“Bacungan has a lot of potential to create these prototypes for sustainable communities,” Villaraza said. “It’s still accessible to the city, but it’s far away enough so that we can see the transition between the modern and the traditional lifestyles.”

He added that Bacungan is home to communities and initiatives striving to protect Palawan from development driven purely by profit, making it a fitting place to demonstrate sustainable living in practice.

Off-grid vision

Rather than using conventional construction methods, Bahay Pangarap was built using mud sourced from the village itself and ecobricks made from plastic bottles tightly packed with nonbiodegradable plastic waste.

Jesharelle Parcia, a Bacungan resident who helped build Bahay Pangarap, admitted she initially doubted the project would be completed because construction stretched over two years with long periods of inactivity.

“I didn’t think Bahay Pangarap would be finished because the progress wasn’t continuous,” Parcia said. “When it was finally completed, it felt fulfilling because we knew we were part of that dream. We stepped on the mud and filled the bottles until it all came together.”

For Graziele Burmann, a member of Maia Earth and a former teacher, the project’s greatest achievement was the enthusiasm it inspired among young people.

“It was really memorable to see their enthusiasm,” Burmann said. “Everyone got curious about ecobricks, the idea of painting with rocks. With time, everyone wanted to be part of it. The plan started small; we didn’t have to force anything, and things just happened naturally. It was just about strengthening the bond within the communities.”

BAHAY PANGARAP. It stands amid the greenery of Bacungan, Puerto Princesa, built through the collective efforts of students, volunteers, and the community using earth and ecobricks. Photo courtesy of Maia Earth Organization Inc.

Learning beyond the classroom

The construction site became an extension of the classroom itself.

“Normally, when you go to school, it’s theoretical,” Villaraza said. “But this project is active-based learning. We’re not just building the school; we’re also training the kids.”

Rhea Mae Tacan, a student at BNHS who helped build Bahay Pangarap, admitted she initially doubted that mud and plastic waste could be turned into a classroom.

“Seeing Bahay Pangarap finished made me realize how much waste we had transformed into something meaningful,” she said. “It showed that we can build without harming the environment.”

The initiative also encouraged residents to rethink plastic waste. Villaraza noted that improperly discarded plastic can persist for centuries, while burning it contributes to carbon emissions. Through ecobricks, he said, waste that would otherwise end up in landfills or the environment became a useful building material.

The impact extended beyond Bahay Pangarap. Villaraza recalled that students from BNHS organized a cleanup drive that reached the entire barangay, demonstrating how environmental stewardship can begin with young people and spread throughout the community.

CREATIVE LEARNING. Children take part in a creative activity at Maia Earth Village, where learning expands beyond conventional classrooms. Photo courtesy of Maia Earth Organization Inc.

Building a different future

For Burmann, however, the project’s lasting legacy is not measured by the classroom’s mud walls but by the mindset it helped cultivate.

“People need to see that it is possible,” she said. “If you don’t change the mindset, if you don’t show that there is a different way to see things, then it’s very hard to change.”

That mindset continues to shape Maia’s work beyond Bahay Pangarap.

The organization is currently building a health and wellness center with barangay partners and doctors to promote nutrition and natural medicine. It is also working with persons deprived of liberty, or PDLs, at Iwahig Prison and Penal Farm, introducing natural building as a therapeutic and rehabilitative activity.

Today, Bahay Pangarap stands as proof that when a community builds together, even discarded waste can become the foundation of dreams. – Rappler.com

Vic Albert Bagaan is a petroleum engineering student at Palawan State University in Puerto Princesa City, Palawan. The development communication editor of Pioneer Publication, he is an Aries Rufo Fellow for 2026.

World.title: When courts, agencies stepped in to block wage hikes
World.content:
Other government bodies, apart from the NWPC and regional boards, blocked supposed wage hikes before

MANILA, Philippines – A month after the “historic” P85 minimum wage hike was promised for workers in Metro Manila, a Pasig City court temporarily halted the rollout.

It came after two construction companies raised concerns that the hike would disrupt projects that already went through bidding.

This is not the first time that a court, other government bodies, or officials intervened and blocked wage increases in the country.

According to the Wage Rationalization Act, the National Wages and Productivity Commission (NWPC) and its regional counterparts can issue wage orders after public hearings, consultations, and deliberative meetings.

Congress may also introduce bills for wage hikes. The President and civil society groups can call on wage policy-making bodies to review and revise wages. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. made the same call in 2024.

The following are the interventions made by agencies and public officials in relation to regional and national wage hikes:

Pasig RTC suspends P85 NCR Wage Hike (2026)

The first tranche of P60 was implemented on July 25, 2026, with the additional P25 scheduled for next year, January 20, 2027.

However, Branch 152 of the Pasig Regional Trial Court issued a temporary restraining order against the regional wage board and the NWPC’s Wage Order No. 27 until August 13, following a petition by two construction companies.

Readycon Trading and Construction Corporation and R-II Builders argued that the sudden increase would affect existing projects that already went through bidding before the announcement. The two companies cautioned that the hike would reduce profits, make them less competitive in bidding, cut jobs, and even suspend operations.

The court found that the implementation may cause irreparable harm, as companies might have to adjust salaries to prevent wage compression.

However, the Federation of Free Workers and the Nagkaisa Labor Coalition pointed out that the order bypasses Article 126 of the Labor Code.

The code states that appeals must be filed with the NWPC or Regional Boards before any court can issue an injunction or temporary restraining order.

A hearing for a longer preliminary injunction was scheduled for August 3.

P100 hike dies after Congress sine die (2025)

A bill to increase the minimum wage by P100 died after the 19th Congress adjourned its annual session. It was the closest legislated increase since the 1989 hike before decentralization through the Wage Rationalization Act.

The 19th Congress had two versions of the hike. Senator Juan Miguel Zubiri filed Senate Bill No. 2534 proposing a P100 daily increase. The House of Representatives also had House Bill No. 11376, which called for a P200 increase in minimum wage.

Another bill must be introduced and passed in the 20th Congress to increase the daily minimum earnings of workers.

COVID-19 pandemic (2020)

During the COVID-19 pandemic, then-Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) secretary Silvestre Bello III discouraged having a minimum wage hike because of the economy’s fragility at the time.

Bello reasoned that job security was more important and that employers might not be able to meet the calls for a wage increase from P537 to around P700. DOLE believed that a hike during the pandemic would be counterproductive and would force micro, small, and medium businesses to close.

He cautioned that petitions made by labor groups to increase wages must be studied.

SC voids Cagayan wage order (2007)

The Supreme Court (SC) in 2007 voided Wage Order No. R02-03, which was issued in 1995.

The Court ruled that the Regional Tripartite Wages and Productivity Board of Region II overstepped its authority by granting an across-the-board wage increase for non-minimum wage earners.

This 1995 wage order implemented a P15 increase across-the-board in the region, regardless of employment status.

The Bankers’ Council for Personnel Management asked the NWPC whether member-banks with head offices in Metro Manila were exempt from the hike since their employees were already paid above the regional minimum wage.

Metrobank filed a petition directly with the Court of Appeals (CA). The CA denied the petition since the company failed to file within the proper period of 15 days after the decision.

Metrobank then elevated the petition to the SC. Years later, the High Court voided the wage increase, but ruled that workers should not be required to refund the amounts they had received and that the minimum wage would remain unchanged at the time.

SC voids rushed Cagayan wage order (1998)

Another wage order in Cagayan once again found itself in the middle of a legal battle. This time, the dispute centered on whether it had been rushed.

In 1994, DOLE discovered that Cagayan Sugar Milling Company (CARSUMCO) did not give the increase to its higher-earning employees and violated Wage Order No. RO2-02.

CARSUMCO filed an appeal, but DOLE ruled that the company had violated the wage order and ordered it to pay the salary deficiency worth P555,133.41.

The regional board later amended the wage order without holding the mandatory public hearings, resulting in the “across-the-board” wage increase in 1995 that Metrobank challenged years later.

After a back-and-forth between the company and DOLE, the SC issued a TRO pending resolution of the matter. In 1998, the SC ruled in favor of CARSUMCO, clearing the original penalty and declaring the wage order null and void. – Rappler.com

World.title: Celebrating John Gokongwei Jr., the man behind the developments
World.content:
Before he became one of the country’s most respected entrepreneurs, John Gokongwei Jr. was a young dreamer whose belief in possibility laid the foundation for generations of Filipinos

Editor’s note: This press release is sponsored by Robinsons Land Corporation and was handled by BrandRap, the sales and marketing arm of Rappler. No member of the news and editorial team participated in the publishing of this piece.

As Robinsons Land celebrates the 100th birth anniversary of its founder, John Gokongwei Jr., it reflects on the values that defined his life and honors his legacy through John Gokongwei Jr. Boulevard, the newly renamed main thoroughfare of Bridgetowne.

Stretching approximately 1 kilometer and connecting Pasig City and Quezon City, the boulevard serves as the central spine of the estate. More than a road, it stands as a reminder of the vision, discipline, and long-term thinking that guided Mr. John throughout his life and continues to shape Robinsons Land today.

Long before Robinsons Land began building malls, homes, offices, hotels, and mixed-use developments across the Philippines, however, its founder was simply a young boy selling basic goods to help support his family.

When his father passed away, Mr. John, as he was fondly called, was only 13. As the eldest child, he suddenly found himself taking on greater responsibility. To earn money for the family, he and his mother cooked peanuts with garlic, packed them in small bags, and sold them, an experience he would later describe as his first as an entrepreneur.

YOUNG JOHN GOKONGWEI JR. A glimpse into the early life of the man who would go on to build some of the Philippines’ most enduring businesses.

By 15, he was waking before dawn and riding his bicycle several kilometers to the public market. There, he sold spools of thread, bars of soap, and candles, often working long after the other vendors had left. He used part of his earnings to buy food and reinvested the rest in more goods to sell.

From those early experiences grew a much larger vision, one grounded in understanding what people needed, creating opportunities, and building for the long term.

Today, visitors driving through John Gokongwei Jr. Boulevard will encounter a modern estate filled with offices, residences, retail destinations, and public spaces. Yet the journey behind the name began far from boardrooms and master-planned developments. It began with a young boy determined to help his family and create opportunities where few existed.

HONORING JOHN GOKONGWEI JR. JG Summit president and CEO Lance Y. Gokongwei and Robinsons Land president and CEO Mybelle V. Aragon-GoBio stand beside the newly inaugurated John Gokongwei Jr. Boulevard in Bridgetowne.

A habit of learning

Hardship taught Mr. John to work hard, use his resources carefully, and keep moving forward. It also taught him to pay close attention to people: what they needed, what they could afford, and what would encourage them to return.

He remained deeply curious throughout his life. During long trading journeys by boat from Cebu to Manila, he spent the time reading books about people, places, and lives beyond his own experience. He later recalled that reading expanded his mind and helped him see possibilities he had not encountered before.

That curiosity became one of his greatest strengths. He studied markets, observed how consumers behaved, and looked for needs that existing businesses were not meeting.

Mr. John was careful with money and deliberate in his decisions, but he was not afraid to act. He reinvested what he earned, studied opportunities closely, and took calculated risks when he saw long-term potential. Rather than pursue quick gains, he focused on building businesses that could remain useful and relevant for generations.

Building around everyday needs

Mr. John’s experience of hardship also gave him an understanding of what access and opportunity could mean to Filipino families.

Across the businesses he founded, this belief took different forms. Affordable food products reached more households. Air travel became accessible to more Filipinos. Educational initiatives helped young people prepare for brighter futures, while growing enterprises created jobs and economic opportunities across the country.

Through Robinsons Land, this same philosophy took physical form.

UNVEILING A LEGACY. Robinsons Land’s key executives stand united beneath the John Gokongwei Jr. Boulevard marker.

The company created places around the everyday lives of people: destinations where families could gather, businesses could flourish, travelers could stay, and communities could grow. Across malls, offices, residences, hotels, logistics facilities, and mixed-use developments, Robinsons Land sought to create environments that support how Filipinos live, work, and connect.

In many ways, Bridgetowne exemplifies this vision. Designed as an integrated community that brings together residential, commercial, office, hospitality, and public spaces, it reflects Mr. John’s belief in creating long-term value through thoughtful planning and connectivity. It is fitting that the estate’s main thoroughfare now bears his name.

A legacy that continues to guide

Since its establishment in 1980, Robinsons Land has grown into one of the country’s leading property developers, with developments spanning malls, offices, residences, hotels, logistics facilities, and integrated estates. While the company has evolved over the decades, many of the principles associated with its founder remain unchanged: understand people’s needs, study opportunities carefully, use resources wisely, and build with the future in mind.

BUILT TO COMMEMORATE. Bridgetowne stands as a testament to Robinsons Land’s commitment to long-term value creation, with John Gokongwei Jr. Boulevard serving as the estate’s central corridor.

The buildings and destinations are the most visible part of what Mr. John helped create. Behind them is a way of thinking formed much earlier, when a young boy learned to turn hardship into opportunity and uncertainty into possibility.

Today, as Robinsons Land marks John Gokongwei Jr.’s 100th birth anniversary and the inauguration of the boulevard that now bears his name, his legacy continues to live on not only through the places that were built, but through the values that continue to guide them. For the generations who will pass through John Gokongwei Jr. Boulevard in the years ahead, it serves as a reminder that meaningful progress begins with vision, perseverance, and the courage to build for the future.

Explore the story of John Gokongwei Jr. and the values that continue to guide Robinsons Land here. – Rappler.com

World.title: 5 students among dead in Baguio landslide
World.content:
LANDSLIDE. Authorities end search, rescue, and retrieval operations at the site of a deadly landslide in Baguio City, August 11, 2026.

‘We ask the entire education community to join us in keeping the families, the victims, and the Cordillera region in our prayers,’ the Department of Education says

MANILA, Philippines – Five young students were among those who died after a landslide struck Barangay Guisad Surong in Baguio City following nonstop rain in the area, the Department of Education (DepEd) said on Tuesday, August 11.

According to the DepEd, among those who died in the tragedy were two Grade 7 students from Guisad Valley National High School; a Grade 3 student and a Grade 4 student from Bonifacio Elementary School; and a student under the Alternative Learning System.

“Nakikiramay po kami nang buong puso (We extend our heartfelt condolences),” the agency said in a statement.

“We ask the entire education community to join us in keeping the families, the victims, and the Cordillera region in our prayers,” it added.

On late Sunday evening, August 9, 13 people were buried by thick mud and debris as the southwest monsoon or habagat battered areas in Luzon. Three houses were hit by the landslide, affecting five families, according to the Baguio City Public Information Office.

Search, rescue, and retrieval operations ended early Tuesday morning. Three people were pulled out alive, while the remaining 10 died in the landslide.

“We grieve with every family who waited and hoped during the search, and we share in the sadness that has settled over our community. Our thoughts and prayers remain with them during this very difficult time,” Baguio City Mayor Benjamin Magalong said in a statement.

Magalong thanked the responders, volunteers, and other personnel for their work, as well as those who reached out to offer food, clothing, supplies, and other forms of assistance.

He said authorities intend to begin cleanup operations once the weather clears out.

“The area remains dangerous, and our teams have observed stress signs in the soil. We do not want to put our personnel, volunteers, or residents at further risk,” the mayor said.

There were also reported deaths after landslides in other parts of the province of Benguet. Two were killed when a landslide buried a roadside eatery in La Trinidad, and two others died while clearing mud near their home in Atok.

Class suspensions, school infra

Meanwhile, the DepEd said face-to-face classes at 9,890 schools across eight regions remain suspended on Tuesday, disrupting the learning of around 6.5 million students.

Some 800 schools in the Ilocos Region have resumed their classes.

More damaged classrooms have also been reported following flooding and landslides triggered by Tropical Storm Maymay (Kujira) and the southwest monsoon.

The DepEd said at least 32 schools were hit by landslides.

As of 8 am on Tuesday, the agency said 3,927 classrooms sustained minor damage, 1,135 had major damage, and 1,093 were “totally damaged.” The figure came from 961 affected schools.

Currently, 522 classrooms in 134 schools have been turned into evacuation centers for more than 2,800 families. – Rappler.com

World.title: How to read what Gabby Lopez, Piki Lopez, and Ramon Ang actually said
World.content:
Every side is telling the public the same thing, that this is a stabilizing, peace-building move, not a takeover. Nothing filed so far proves or disproves that. What comes next will show whether it holds.

On Monday, August 10, statements about the sale of a quarter of Lopez Inc. to businessman Ramon S. Ang landed one after another over roughly 7 hours, from a one-line board resignation filed at 8:03 am to a warmer statement past 3 pm. Something was being said all at once, by several people who do not normally coordinate, and the way it landed together says as much as any single document does on its own.

Read individually, each statement is a small piece of news. Read together, for the themes that repeat across them, they tell a reader what the people at the center of the Lopez family dispute actually want the public to take away from that day, and where the limits of what they’re willing to say sit.

Continuity is the message

The clearest theme is continuity.

“The family branches that continue to hold the controlling majority of Lopez Inc., will continue to lead it,” said Ang, who bought the stake personally rather than through San Miguel Corporation, the conglomerate he runs.

Federico “Piki” Lopez, whom his majority cousins in Lopez Inc. board voted to remove as president in February 2026 but who has remained in the post under a court injunction blocking that removal, makes a version of the same reassurance in a different key. Welcoming Ang “with deep appreciation,” he frames the entry as consistent with “our history of partnering with recognized individuals and institutions to promote the growth of our businesses,” anchoring the deal to precedent rather than announcing anything new.

The plainest statement of the morning came first: a one-sentence disclosure First Philippine Holdings (FPH) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), confirming that Roberta L. Feliciano had resigned from its board, citing the sale of Crème Investment Corporation’s (Crème) shares in Lopez Inc. as her reason. Crème is the holding vehicle for the heirs of Eugenio “Geny” Lopez Jr., representing their branch’s 25.68% stake in Lopez, Inc., the private company that sits at the apex of the Lopez Group’s shareholder structure. Feliciano’s resignation confirmed what had circulated as rumor before that morning: a sale had happened at the very top of that structure. Its plain, procedural tone set up the warmer statements that followed from the rest of the family.

A deal described as friendship, not finance

A second theme is how personal and relational the language is, and how little of it is financial. None of the three men’s quotes mention a price, a valuation, or what the stake is worth. What they mention instead is how long they have known each other.

Gabby Lopez: “Our families have known Ramon a long time. I am confident he will be a good partner to Lopez, Inc.”

Piki Lopez: “We have been friends for a long time and so I do look forward to working together with him.”

Ramon Ang: “I have known the Lopez family for decades. Not one branch of it, but all of them. I am a friend to each, and I intend to stay that way.”

A transaction involving a quarter of one of the country’s largest, and most colorful, private holding companies is being described in the vocabulary of an old friendship rather than a deal.

San Miguel Corporation’s own letter to the stock exchange backs the same framing from the institutional side rather than the personal one, confirming that Ang bought the stake “in his personal capacity through Illumina Investment Holdings, Inc., a corporation wholly owned by Mr. Ang,” executed “upon the invitation of the ELopez Family,” and separate from San Miguel itself, whose board he would only brief on the purchase days later.

The press statements and disclosures to the exchange are making the identical point: this was not San Miguel’s move, and Ang did not go looking for it either. The family asked him in.

The vocabulary of progress, not an ending

A third theme runs through the choice of verbs. Peace, resolving, stronger, partner, growth. Every one of them points forward, and none of them points to a finish line.

Gabby put it plainly: “This dispute has not been good for any of us, or for the people who work in our companies. This allows us to take a step towards the restoration of family peace.” A step, not the restoration itself. Piki calls it “a great step toward resolving issues,” not the resolution. Ang says his interest is that the group “comes out of this stronger,” a phrase that assumes an ongoing process rather than a closed chapter. What none of the three men reaches for is reconciliation.

That distinction matters for those trying to make sense of a family dispute mostly through statements like these. Advisors who study conflicts at this stage draw a hard line between the two ideas: peace means there is no longer a shared stake left to fight over. As long as both branches held shares in the same company, every board vote, every capital decision, every disagreement about strategy gave the conflict a fresh trigger, because each side’s decisions affected the other’s investment whether they agreed with those decisions or not. Once one branch sells out entirely, that shared terrain disappears, and so does the machinery that kept generating new rounds of the fight.

Reconciliation means the relationship itself is repaired. A family branch can secure the first without achieving the second, and it does so by selling its way out of the shared stake. Everything in Gabby’s own statement suggests that is exactly the transaction he is describing. He is not saying the feud is over. He is saying his branch is no longer inside it.

An exit, not a rebalancing

That extends to the other half of Gabby’s statement, the line that could otherwise pass as an afterthought: the sale “allows me to channel our family’s resources into businesses aligned with our personal mission.” That sounds like portfolio housekeeping, one branch trimming an old holding to fund something new.

That housekeeping likely points toward ABS-CBN.

Lopez Inc. holds roughly 79% of the network’s voting rights against a smaller economic stake, closer to 56%, a gap that exists because of how the company’s preferred shares carry voting parity without matching cash-flow rights. ABS-CBN also sits closer to Gabby’s branch of the family than to Piki’s.

Gabby is the eldest of the current third generation descended from Eugenio “Geny” Lopez Jr., and that line has long been identified with the network, a news organization built on a reputation for reporting on the powerful, and has an entertainment content powerhouse alongside it. It is also the network that lost its congressional franchise in 2020, under the Duterte administration, which had repeatedly and publicly criticized both ABS-CBN and the Lopez family, a decision that forced the network off free-to-air broadcast.

But everything else in his statement points the same way: the talk of family peace, the years of dispute behind it, the fact that he is leaving rather than staying to negotiate a settlement with his cousins. A branch that walks away from a fight it no longer wants to win is not adjusting its portfolio. It is exiting the fight itself.

Put together, the five separate statements agree on four things: nothing structural changed, Ang was invited rather than the one who came looking, the relationships involved go back decades, and none of them call this an ending.

What remains unanswered

Four questions stand out.

The first is price. Lopez Inc. is private, so there is no market quote to check the sale against, no ticker that moved. Whatever Ang paid for 25.68% would say something none of the five statements do: what the underlying interests in the listed units — Lopez Holdings, ABS-CBN Corp, ABS-CBN Holdings Corp, First Philippine Holdings, First Gen, and Rockwell Land — are worth in someone’s actual accounting, and whether Ang negotiated a discount for buying into a company that has spent the better part of a year in public family litigation.

The second is what the shares Ramon Ang bought actually carry. Owning 25.68% of a company can mean almost nothing beyond a claim on dividends, or it can come with a board seat, a veto over major decisions, or a say in who runs the company next. Nothing in the five statements says which. Ang’s own line, that the branches holding the controlling majority “will continue to lead” Lopez Inc., answers only who runs the company day to day. It says nothing about whether Ang can block a decision, demand information from the company, or has a formal vote the next time Lopez Inc. makes a decision as big as this one.

The third is the ownership table itself. This dispute has been described for months as a 71-29 split between two cousin blocs, but that shorthand no longer describes Lopez Inc.: Créme’s 25.68%, once part of the 71% figure, now belongs to Ang. The two-bloc description this Lopez family feud series and others have used since the feud became public needs to be retired, or at least qualified, from here on.

The fourth question is simple to ask and hard to answer: will this trigger a mandatory tender offer?

Lopez Inc. itself is private, so the sale by itself needs no tender offer. But it sits above six listed companies: Lopez Holdings, ABS-CBN Corp, ABS-CBN Holdings Corp, First Philippine Holdings, First Gen, and Rockwell Land. Philippine securities rules can still require a tender offer when someone gains effective control of a listed company indirectly, through its parent, rather than by buying shares on the exchange itself. That is what “indirect acquisition” means here, and it’s worth explaining because it’s the only reason a private sale two levels up the chain could carry public consequences for six listed companies at all.

Whether that applies to Ang’s purchase depends on a distinction the five statements do not settle: has he bought only a minority stake in Lopez Inc., or has he gained something closer to control over the listed companies beneath it. The percentage alone cannot answer that. It requires the deed of assignment, whatever shareholders’ agreement exists, and whatever the Philippine Stock Exchange and SEC eventually require Lopez Inc. or its subsidiaries to disclose.

As of this writing, none of that documentation is public. There is no stock-and-transfer-book confirmation of the transfer, no disclosed purchase price, no disclosed exact Lopez Inc. share count, no disclosed shareholders’ agreement. No representative of the Manolo or Prescy Psinakis branches has resigned a board seat the way Feliciano did. No fresh SEC or court filing has altered the legal posture of the broader family dispute.

Here is what that gap means: every side is telling the public the same thing, that this is a stabilizing, peace-building move, not a takeover. Nothing filed so far proves or disproves that. What comes next will show whether it holds. Watch for a board-seat change at Lopez, Inc. itself, or a move in the pending litigation and SEC matters. Until one of those happens, August 10 was a day when five people and institutions, speaking in five different tones, worked with unusual care to say the same thing. The rest, we don’t know yet. – Rappler.com

Lala Rimando wrote about Philippine business, and managed newsrooms, including Newsbreak, ABS-CBN, Rappler, and Forbes, for over 25 years. She’s now based in La Union, taking care of her mom with dementia, and working on the multimedia biography of the late John Gokongwei.
