World.title: 'Evidence is clear': Players association says brutal schedule behind injuries
World.content:
The Professional Tennis Players Association (PTPA) believes a string of withdrawals from the Canadian Open underscore concerns that professional tennis's lengthy calendar and expanded top-level events are increasing injury risks.

The players' advocacy group said it was saddened but not surprised by the absences from the tournament, arguing that reduced recovery time between tournaments was contributing to injuries occurring earlier in the season and becoming more serious.

The Canadian Open men's event in Montreal was hit by the withdrawals of world number one Jannik Sinner and 24-time grand slam champion Novak Djokovic, while Carlos Alcaraz was also sidelined with a wrist injury. Hometown favourite Felix Auger-Aliassime also pulled out due to a back injury before his opening match.

On the women's side, defending champion Victoria Mboko, Wimbledon finalist Karolina Muchova, Emma Raducanu and Jasmine Paolini are also missing the tournament with injuries.

The first quarterfinal matches of the tournament begin later on Tuesday AEST.

Tournament organisers said last month that recurring late withdrawals from Masters 1000 events had become a wider issue for the sport.

PTPA says 'evidence is clear'

The PTPA said it had collected and analysed injury data from more than 30,000 professional matches across all levels of the game over the past eight years in a project launched three years ago with its medical director, Dr Robby Sikka.

'Not ready to compete': Sinner pulls out of tournament ahead of US Open Men's tennis world number one Jannik Sinner pulls out of the Cincinnati Open with a right knee injury, handing the Italian a blow in his preparations for this month's US Open.

"The evidence is clear: the season is too long, recovery time is shrinking, and injuries are occurring earlier and becoming more severe," the PTPA said in a statement posted on social media.

The group said upper-body injuries were up 42 per cent in the first quarter of 2026 compared with the same period in 2025, according to its analysis. Arm injuries were up 112 per cent this year compared with the 2025 average, it added.

The ATP expanded seven of its nine Masters 1000 tournaments to 12-day events under its OneVision strategic plan, with 2025 the first season in which the longer format was used across those events.

The PTPA said the change had cut into the time players have to rest, train and travel between tournaments, despite players having voiced concerns about the demands of the schedule for years.

"Short-term commercial interests cannot come at the expense of player health," the association said. "Protecting players isn't just about today's competitors, it is about protecting the future of tennis."

Schedule the players' choice

The ATP has previously said players retain choices over their schedules and that it is working to create incentives for an appropriate number of matches to be played during the season.

Spokespeople for the ATP and WTA Tours did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The PTPA called for the sport to take a player-health and data-driven approach to restructuring the calendar.

It said players should have a meaningful role in shaping the schedule, while mandatory tournament commitments should be reduced to allow adequate recovery.

It also urged the ATP to consider reversing the 12-day Masters 1000 format.

Reuters

World.title: Bird flu drives a 50 per cent cost increase for badminton players
World.content:
While bird flu has only landed on Australian shores in the last few months, a group of sportsmen and women have been feeling its impact for years.

The deadly strain of H5 avian influenza has riddled wild and domesticated avian species across the world, with the total number of dead birds in the hundreds of millions.

While the spread of the disease has Australians across science and agriculture increasingly concerned, the nation's badminton players have long counted its costs.

The mass culling of flocks of geese and poultry across east and central Asia in recent years has massively cut the global supply of feathers critical to making the shuttlecocks needed for any game of the racquet sport to go ahead.

Countries across the world have culled birds to manage H5N1 outbreaks. (Reuters: Luc Gnago)

Shuttlecock shock

The impact has seen equipment costs skyrocket for badminton clubs across the country.

A high-quality shuttlecock uses 16 feathers from the left wing of either a duck or a goose, though each bird can only supply two to three feathers that meet specifications.

China is home to most of the world's poultry farms where the specific feathers are harvested, leaving the product exposed to major price fluctuations pinned to the health of the birds.

Goose feathers are at a premium as healthy flocks become rarer. (ABC Great Southern: Eliza Kavanagh)

Badminton Australia chief executive Tjitte Weistra says even a mid-range shuttle, such as the Yonex AS-30, has become near-unaffordable for most players and clubs.

"A decade ago a tube of a dozen AS-30s would sit from $30 to $35. That's now well over $70," he said.

"This means the cost of hosting a tournament or even club play can get very, very expensive."

Tjitte Weistra said synthetic shuttles are not yet good enough for most players. (Supplied: Tjitte Weistra)

Great Southern Badminton Association chair Michelle Watson said her organisation spends $3,000 on shuttles every four to six months.

Nightly fees have had to rise to maintain quality equipment with synthetic alternatives not an option.

Michelle Watson (right) says increasing costs have been challenging for local players. (Supplied: Michelle Watson)

"Feathers are what the game should be played with and are far superior," she said.

"Players that understand the game and play more than at a social level expect quality shuttles.

" I believe synthetics will be the way of the future due to feathers being unsustainable [but] they are currently not close to where they need to be to be an appropriate option. "

WA players particularly hard-hit

Metamorph Shuttle director Ryan Zengyuan said WA's near-total reliance on imported equipment left local players even more exposed.

"An agricultural supply crash in Asia instantly triggers inventory shortages and doubles prices for local players," Mr Zengyuan said.

"[As a result] local sport retailers have been forced to increase retail prices by 30 to 50 per cent over the last few years to cover the skyrocketing cost of raw feathers and international freight."

Players say you cannot replicate the flight of natural feather shuttles. (ABC Great Southern: Will Corbett)

While bird flu has decimated the global feather market, freight costs, oil prices and competition for the cork used in the head of the shuttle are additional factors in the rising prices.

Seeking alternatives

Mr Weistra said local clubs are starting to look at alternative options to curb the price rise, including players making peace with synthetic shuttles.

"They're trying to get cheaper feather shuttles which don't have the same characteristics," he said.

" In the past, they just weren't open to it because the crisis wasn't big enough. But now the cost is becoming really prohibitive. "

"I guess they are inclined to look at alternative options and accept that maybe they're not perfect, but it will do for now."

World.title: Major football bodies pen letter seeking Infantino exit over 'deception'
World.content:
UEFA, CONCACAF and the AFC believe FIFA President Gianni Infantino's recent plan to sell an interest in the World Cup was a "fundamental breach of trust" with the institutions world soccer's governing body serves.

In an "open letter to the football family", the governing bodies also said that "when trust is broken through deception, when an individual places himself above the collective that entrusted him with authority, that duty has been abandoned."

UEFA runs football in Europe, CONCACAF does the same for North, Central America and the Caribbean, while the AFC governs the sport in Asia.

FIFA pledges 'full support' for Infantino and apologises for sell-off plan FIFA has reiterated its support for embattled president Gianni Infantino, while apologising to its member associations for the aborted bid to sell off stakes in the World Cup.

The letter was co-signed by UEFA President Aleksander Čeferin, AFC President Salman Bin Ibrahim Al-Khalifa, CONCACAF President Victor Montagliani and three general secretaries.

"Football is the world's greatest shared passion. It belongs to no individual and no institution. It belongs to the players, the fans, the clubs, the member associations and every institution entrusted with safeguarding its future," the open letter said.

"It is in that spirit, as confederations representing its members, that we speak collectively today."

Infantino is facing a revolt after his failed plan to sell stakes in the World Cup to private equity investors.

"It is not the conduct of a custodian of the game, but of one who believes the game is answerable to him," the letter said.

"These are not the qualities football deserves in its leadership. That is why we have taken this stance: not lightly and not alone, but together, and out of duty to the game we serve."

Australia's Socceroos also fall under the AFC, which has spoken out against Infantino. (Getty Images: Xinhua/Ziyu Julian Zhu)

UEFA previously issued a threat to boycott the World Cup and other FIFA competitions despite the governing body abandoning and apologising for its failed plan.

Norway's football federation called for Infantino to step down, while the English Football Association has also withdrawn its support for his re-election next March.

"Football's strength has always been its unity. We call for that unity to be honoured now," the letter said. "For leadership that serves football, not seeks to command it."

Last Wednesday, FIFA said it had apologised for errors made over the failed plan but that senior staff at a crisis meeting in Morocco "reaffirmed their full support" for his presidency.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

However, the nature of the meeting was also met with criticism.

"FIFA's own letter also confirms that only one elected official was present at the leadership meeting in Morocco," the open letter said.

"No FIFA Council members or Member Associations were invited to participate. Only the management committee, composed of FIFA-employed senior staff, was present."

FIFA was also urged to go further than just acknowledging mistakes were made.

"It treats this as a failure of communication, when what football witnessed was a failure of judgement," the letter said.

"There remains no recognition that attempting to sell an interest in the FIFA World Cup was a profound failure of judgement — not just a procedural misstep, but a fundamental breach of trust with the very institutions FIFA exists to serve."

In a statement Saturday, FIFA defended Infantino against what it called a "concerted and ongoing effort" to undermine his leadership of the organisation.

That statement followed a report by British newspaper The Daily Telegraph raising questions about an exit package paid by UEFA to a female staffer who worked with Infantino when he was general secretary of European soccer's ruling body.

UEFA confirmed a "departure payment" was made to the employee and said it was "in line" with regulations at the time.

Infantino worked at UEFA for 16 years before being elected FIFA president.

World.title: Big Tex leaves big impact on and off the field
World.content:
Taylor Walker's legacy is littered with athletic greatness and career-defining goals but his impact off the field and in the community makes him a true champion.

Nineteen years ago, a boy from Broken Hill with tips in his hair and a room littered with Crows posters crossed the border to pursue a dream.

The man affectionately known as Tex, after Chuck Norris' iconic character, was a 75-kilogram prospect who'd only ever wanted to be a footballer.

"When I arrived here as a skinny kid from Broken Hill, I never imagined where this journey would take me," Walker said on Monday.

"Football has given me so much but more than anything it's given me people."

Walker — who yesterday announced he would be retiring at season's end — was the final pick in the 2007 draft, but had to wait as Melbourne and Fremantle passed their final selections before the Adelaide Crows took a punt on an injured prospect who had been injured riding his motocross bike shortly after making the NSW Under-16 squad.

Walker joined the Crows as a "skinny kid from Broken Hill". (Supplied: Gavin Schmidt)

What followed was a rollercoaster journey of growth, leadership and legacy.

"His stats tell a story … but that is just part of his story," Crows CEO Tim Silvers said on Monday.

"He's been a great person, a wonderful leader, and he's led through the ups and downs of our footy club. He's led with strength, resilience, passion and determination.

" We're really proud of what he's done, the human he's become and the family man he is. "

Adelaide coach Matthew Nicks echoed those sentiments, saying Walker's legacy at West Lakes is the greatest of any Crow in club history.

"I don't think there's been anyone bigger, when you talk about the impact he's had — not just on football, but on this state and our supporter base," Nicks said.

An emerging talent

It was a perfect storm that landed Walker at West Lakes. The AFL was eager to expand its growth areas in New South Wales and launched a scholarship program requiring clubs to take two players from the state.

Junior scout Mark Ross was sent to the region and caught a glimpse of a young man who would become Adelaide's all-time leading goalkicker.

Thankfully for recruiting boss Hamish Ogilvie, his injury meant no-one else got to see his potential ahead the draft.

Walker takes a mark in front of Port Adelaide's Paul Stewart during a 2011 Showdown. (AAP Image: Ben Macmahon)

It wasn't all smooth sailing for the soon-to-be seven-time leading goalkicker. After kicking over 50 goals in the SANFL for Norwood, Walker was given a debut against Collingwood in the first round of 2009, recording five touches and a goal in a thrilling four-point win.

But his 14-game debut season ended in the reserves and numerous omissions in 2010 as the young forward clashed with coach Neil Craig over his defensive pressure.

Premiership Crow and former Adelaide board member Rod Jameson remembers his treatment being unique for key forwards at the time.

"Neil Craig made it hard for him. They sent him back to work on his defensive game which was rarely heard of then," Jameson said.

" He'd go back and still kick numerous goals. We all knew there was talent there but it was the timing and consistency. "

There were rumours of a move to expansion club GWS and an omission after being caught on live TV drinking a beer at the SANFL — but the appointment of Brenton Sanderson as Adelaide's head coach in 2012 proved a turning point.

Walker watches from the player's bench after injuring his knee in 2013. (Joe Castro: AAP Image)

A 63-goal season led to a runner-up finish in the Coleman Medal and it felt like South Australia's next big thing had arrived, but an ACL injury early in 2013 was a devastating blow.

"I always tried to look at it glass half full … you've always got a choice to make. You can sit and sulk and look at the negatives or get on with life and do something about it," Walker said.

"You go through challenges in your career that make you want to get better."

Securing the captaincy

Walker's optimism and determination saw him return early in the 2014 season and inspired his teammates to appoint him captain the following year.

His first season at the helm was one of the most difficult any leader could have faced, with the tragic death of senior coach Phil Walsh.

But Walker was able to unite a shattered playing group and guide them into three consecutive finals series that culminated in the club's first grand final in 20 years and back-to-back AFLPA best captain awards.

The Crows got close to a premiership in 2017, but Richmond proved too good on the day. (AAP: Julian Smith)

Jameson recalls Walker's maturity and guidance in the club's darkest period being an inspiration to a devastated community.

"At heart he's a larrikin … [but] he says and does things that the group is able to follow, and it's a special trait," he said.

"The passing of Walshy and the grand final hardship … it wasn't easy but that's how you learn.

"He's just a ripping bloke. It's what good clubs are made of — they're the building blocks you want in the club. To build connections and catchers, he's gone about it his way and it's been an incredible career."

Walker himself believed the experience gave him perspective and pride.

"One of Walshy's favourite sayings was just get the job done," Walker said.

"If he was looking down he would've been incredibly proud of what we were able to do in that time.

" Life is hard, it's challenging. Things happen that you can't control. Don't take it too seriously. Have fun along the way because it's so short. "

Challenges on and off the field

Entering 2020, the winds of change had struck West Lakes, with coach Don Pyke stepping aside for Matthew Nicks, and Walker handing over the captaincy to Rory Sloane.

Walker faced concerns over his own future, battling a knee injury and engulfed in a racism scandal that saw him suspended for six matches for delivering a slur to North Adelaide's Robbie Young.

"That was an incredibly difficult time for my family and … I learned that words don't just hurt one person, they can hurt so many different people," he said on Monday.

"I'm a better person for that mistake I made. I wish it never happened but also I feel like I'm better for it."

Walker shakes hands with North Adelaide's Robbie Young in the aftermath of the 2021 incident. (Adelaide Football Club)

A refreshed strength and conditioning program not only wound back the clock but saw Walker soar to career highs, with a 76-goal season in 2023 and his first All-Australian blazer.

Firmly in the premiership window after a minor premiership in 2025, Walker was hell-bent on helping the club break its near three-decade long drought but as the injuries rose and the weekly recovery got harder, the decision arrived at 3am last Tuesday.

"The closer I've gotten to the end it's probably become more evident it might be this year but I've treated it like my last year for the past six years," Walker said.

"I knew it was the right time for me and the football club to retire at the end of the year, hopefully with a premiership medallion around my neck.

"I might go out with a bang."

Walker celebrates a Showdown victory in 2018. (Getty Images: AFL Media/James Elsby)

Leaving a legacy

Walker's influence and impact will forever be etched into South Australian footy folklore, with a club record 706 goals and counting, and over 300 games that will see him finish third all-time.

"He's up there with the greats of the club. His impact, his longevity and his leadership," Jameson said.

"When you reflect on the stats and what he's been able to accomplish — he puts himself up in the elite category."

"Everyone sees the goals and big moments but those who have worked closely with Tex know the care he has for his teammates, our coaches and staff, and the club," Nicks said.

"He's someone who led through actions as much as words. He was prepared to stand up when things were going well and, importantly, he stood tall when they weren't."

Taylor Walker and Crows coach Matthew Nicks in 2020. (AAP: David Mariuz)

A clash with the ladder-leading Fremantle Dockers awaits Friday night as the Crows fight for a top-four finish, but when it's all said and done Walker will finish thankful for the opportunity to represent his childhood club.

"I've had three loves in my life — my family, my friends and footy," he said.

"I want to go back [to Broken Hill] and win a premiership there. Coaching is on the radar but I want to take a deep breath.

World.title: Dog hurt in race marketed as opposing Tasmania's racing ban
World.content:
A greyhound has suffered a fall and injury at a regional New South Wales race named in solidarity with Tasmania's racing industry, which faces a possible statewide ban.

WARNING: This story contains images that may cause distress for some readers.

It was race two on Sunday night in the town of Temora.

The race, named "We Stand With Tasmania Pathways", was a 330-metre dash to the finish for seven greyhounds.

Five-year-old greyhound Manila Shelby bolted from the box and collided with another dog at the first turn.

She was flung into the side metal barrier and struggled to get back up.

A stewards' report from the night said it was likely she broke her shoulder blade and injured her "tricep".

A Greyhound Racing NSW spokesperson later said the trainer took his dog to the vet the following day and an examination and x-rays showed no fractures.

Manila Shelby was given oral medication and will not be able to race for several weeks, vet notes shared by Greyhound Racing NSW showed.

The race replay video has been deleted from the state's racing website.

On a prominent betting site, the race replay has also been edited to exclude the fall.

It is one of several races called "We Stand With Tasmania" that have resulted in falls and injuries.

Loading...

On December 22, 2025, during race three at Maitland in NSW, Hey Pat fell and sustained a serious foreleg fracture.

The greyhound is now listed as deceased.

Two greyhounds fell on October 20 last year during race one in Nowra, NSW.

And during race five in Warragul, Victoria, on October 23, Collinda Blinder fell and tumbled after the first turn.

Printed caps in support of Tasmania's greyhound industry have been spotted track-side. (Supplied)

The race where Manila Shelby was injured has been uploaded to Greyhound Racing SA's website.

In Tasmania, when a dog is injured on the track, a video of the race is never uploaded.

The Tasmanian industry's peak body Tasracing said this decision is made out of respect to the industry, as well as the greyhound trainer and animal involved.

Tasmanian Greens animal rights spokesperson Cassy O'Connor said the race was "horrible viewing" and "characteristic of the dangerous conditions greyhounds are forced to race in".

"This is happening in our name as Tasmanians," Ms O'Connor said.

"Manila Shelby isn't the first greyhound to be injured in mainland races under the 'Stand With Tasmania' banner, and sadly, she won't be the last.

"But we have the power to stop greyhounds being put in harm's way in this state."

Five-year-old greyhound Manila Shelby sustained injuries during a race in Temora, New South Wales, on August 9, 2026. (Supplied)

The greyhound races authorities don't want you to see If you watched greyhound race videos on Tasracing's website, you would likely never know that dozens of dogs were injured or killed during events last year.

The state government has committed to cutting funding to the industry from 2029, which coincides with the end of the current funding deal for the code.

Premier Jeremy Rockliff said in August last year "it was time to make a call on the future of the sport", and he "continues to be concerned about animal welfare".

"It's time to draw a line in the sand and ensure an orderly exit from greyhound racing in Tasmania," Mr Rockliff said at the time.

Tasmanian Premier Jeremy Rockliff with a greyhound (Facebook: Jeremy Rockliff)

Legislation to phase out the industry passed the Tasmanian parliament's lower house in December 2025, but was pulled from the upper house after the state government feared it didn't have the numbers to pass.

"Greyhound racing is out of step with community expectations. It does not prioritise animal welfare," Tasmanian Liberal MP Marcus Vermey said.

Tasmanian Labor continues to support the industry.

Editor's note 11/8/26: A previous version of this story said the greyhound Manila Shelby was 'badly injured' based on a stewards report that mentioned suspected fractures. Greyhound Racing NSW later provided a statement and vet notes and the story was updated to reflect that a fracture was not found.

Tech.title: Mark Zuckerberg doesn’t understand how to live
Tech.content:
Recently, a man I was rock climbing with told me about how he’d used AI to make a motivational poster for himself, which he’d hung on his bedroom wall: a bear, walking a slackline over a canyon, holding a sign that said, “Do cool shit.” I made what I hoped was a polite noise. What reaction was this man looking for? He probably hoped someone, maybe me, would say it was cool or inspiring. It seemed I was not the first person he’d told about this poster. “You know, it’s funny,” he said to me. “No one ever says anything about it.”

I have been thinking about this now for several days. There’s a sort of turducken of things that I find off-putting all rolled into this anecdote: hippie shit, motivational posters, AI “art.” Still, the sum total of reactions to this poster appears to be polite noises.

But what is the correct answer to someone showing you their slop? No one made it. Even bad art — for instance, a version of that motivational poster drawn by a person — requires effort on the part of the artist, and expresses the artist’s mind, both in the content and in the motor skills required to draw lines on a page. It requires a person’s time and attention. AI “art” requires typing a prompt into a box, and maybe refining the results a couple times. There’s nothing to react to.

Zuckerberg is trying to be the soothing tech guru

I bring this up because Mark Zuckerberg has posted a manifesto that he — or his communications team, or possibly an AI — wrote. The point of this 6,500-word essay is to define a positive future for AI. It strikes me as an inauspicious sign for AI that a new, supposedly world-changing and value-creating technology should need such a defense, but AI has been getting bad press these days. People hate data centers, and the higher electricity bills that come with them. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has said the technology may cause “unusually painful” job losses across multiple industries. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman’s house was the target of, first, a Molotov cocktail, and then gunfire.

“It is surprising that the discourse from many developing AI is so filled with doom,” the essay says. “I do not understand why anyone who believes that AI will eliminate most jobs and much of humanity’s relevance would rush to build that future.”

I find it difficult to believe that Zuckerberg doesn’t have Amodei’s phone number. Or Altman’s. I know he has Elon Musk’s — I’ve seen their texts in court. Perhaps he should have texted them to ask!

Anyway, Zuckerberg is trying to be the soothing tech guru, here to tell us that things are going to be okay. He’s addressing, however belatedly, the rage that many people feel about AI. There are sections on data centers (Meta is building power sources for some data centers in the future, but don’t ask for renewable energy) and “preventing government tyranny.” This essay exists to try to quiet the AI backlash — even if it never quite says that directly.

Love is not just a feeling; it is a way of paying attention

We will leave aside the question of “superintelligence,” which is Zuckerberg’s preferred term for what the rest of the industry calls “artificial general intelligence”; let’s stipulate, for the purposes of this essay, that it is indeed possible to create. I am also going to ignore the risible defense of the pervert glasses contained in this piece; they are indefensible. As for the risks, I think they are best addressed elsewhere. What I am interested in is what Zuckerberg — or whoever is writing for him — believes will improve all our lives.

Here is his first pitch: “Everyone will have an exceptionally capable personal agent that understands you, your goals, and everything you care about. Your agent will work 24/7 on your behalf to improve your relationships, health, career, finances, home management, hobbies, and more.” I am struck, here, by the inclusion of “relationships” and “hobbies.”

What strengthens a relationship? Almost always, it is personal investment. Perhaps an AI agent might be better at predicting what my father will want for his birthday than I am, but it definitionally cannot give him my time and consideration. Love is not just a feeling; it is a way of paying attention.

Zuckerberg’s vision of maximizing productivity comes at the cost of my experience

Zuckerberg uses an example that is telling, in a grim kind of way: He asked an AI to pick out a “personalized” recipe to bake with his daughter. He could have considered what kind of baking his daughter enjoys, what her skill set is and what he might be able to teach her, then picked a recipe. Maybe he would have picked a bad recipe, and they would have bungled it — but that might have been a fun experience and a good story. Or maybe he would have picked a family recipe, and it would have given him the opportunity to tell her about when he was a child, or what his grandmother was like. Certainly he’s a busy man, but wouldn’t that make the gift of his attention to her hobby even more precious? Perhaps he might have come to understand her better by spending more time thinking about what she likes. Without that attention, the baking they do together seems more focused on accomplishment than quality time.

Relatedly, the point of a hobby is that you do it. Granted, many of my hobbies are physical activities — hiking, running, yoga, rock climbing (with guys who make bad AI art, apparently). But an AI cannot read a book for me, because the activity of reading a book is absorbing its words into my mind; a summary doesn’t do the same thing as the opening lines of Renata Adler’s Speedboat: “Nobody died that year. Nobody prospered. There were no births or marriages. Seventeen reverent satires were written — disrupting a cliché and, presumably, creating a genre.” The summary cannot summon the mood, nor the actual pleasure of reading the words themselves. An AI cannot replicate the soothing quality of knitting my own scarf; it is the knitting itself that soothes.

Zuckerberg suggests that using an AI to assist me in these tasks will let me accomplish more, and that is probably the case. But I always thought the point of a hobby was to relax and enjoy myself. It’s certainly not to maximize productivity. And Zuckerberg’s vision of maximizing productivity comes at the cost of my experience.

This is the guy that had every resource anyone could wish for at his fingertips and his metaverse still flopped

The second thing Zuckerberg presents is “Everyone will have incredible tools for creation to express your ideas.” I would suggest that everyone already has incredible tools for creation to express their ideas, and that one need merely practice with those tools in order to get better at them. The pleasure of, say, learning to make a video is, first of all, making the video itself — who hasn’t had fun goofing around with friends while filming? But it is also getting better at the tools one uses to make the video, and looking back at one’s efforts as one’s directorial eye improves. Sure, this is time-consuming and requires effort — it can’t be done in a single evening — but isn’t that what makes it rewarding?

Similarly, Zuckerberg introduces the unimpressive notion that everyone gets “powerful tools to create new businesses.” This is the guy that had every resource anyone could wish for at his fingertips and his metaverse still flopped. Maybe more ideas can turn into businesses, but not every idea will be a successful business, and the sheer volume of competition may make it much harder to succeed. That is, assuming those powerful tools work as promised. After all, just recently, Meta announced that its AI had hacked another company, following similar incidents from OpenAI and Anthropic. Not only will your own personal company have to deal with such hackers, you may inadvertently engage in corporate espionage yourself. Is that really what every entrepreneur wants to 

Let’s move on to the next absurd idea the manifesto introduces: Everyone gets a “personalized tutor and coach with a PhD in every subject.” Again, for the sake of this essay, pretend that is possible. We have already tried computerized learning, in 2020, and if I recall correctly, it was a spectacular failure. People don’t like it. Kids don’t like it. Teachers are still coping with the fallout. And I hate to do another victory lap on behalf of Aristotle, but it sure seems like having a mentor (phronimos) is really important when it comes to learning, ethical or otherwise. The social part of learning — whether that’s the peer pressure of being in a class, or the need to impress someone you admire — seems indispensable to the experience.

Everyone is equal in AI but some people (the ones with money) are more equal than others

The strongest thing that Zuckerberg suggests, in my view, is the notion that everyone can benefit from and contribute to scientific advances. Now, I benefited from the polio vaccine — among other scientific advances — at least in part because Jonas Salk chose to make it available to everyone without earning any money from it. But never mind that. I am curious about what it means to contribute to scientific advances in this sense.

Zuckerberg gives some vague handwaving about personalized therapies, which have long been a goal in medicine. Again, let’s assume AI can even do this. I notice, however, that personalization is possible only when doctors have enough time to actually listen to their patients. It also means that patients will need to have the means to pay for personalized medicine, whether through their insurance or otherwise. But this bit from the essay is vague enough that he may actually mean that AI will allow researchers to harvest samples from all of us and test things more quickly, which has its own haunting privacy implications, especially coming from Mark Zuckerberg.

For his final point, Zuckerberg outlines the current state of affairs: Everyone is equal in AI but some people (the ones with money) are more equal than others. The best models will remain paywalled, accessible only to the rich. But what if everyone had free access, he wonders. You mean like they do right now, Mark? How on earth does making the status quo permanent improve our lives?

Consider all this against Terence Tao’s narrower vision of what AI is for in mathematics. He asks us to imagine the following statement is true: “AI tools will, reasonably soon, become capable of performing a reasonable fraction of research-level mathematical tasks, with reasonable levels of success, quality, supervision, and cost.” Tao then stops and asks a crucial question: What are our goals?

I am coming to believe we need a better quality of AI booster

It is the question that Zuckerberg’s vision of the future doesn’t ask. For each thing Zuckerberg outlines as a possibility, the presumed outcome is some kind of accomplishment. The possibility of pleasure, of experience, of self-knowledge or self-expression are missing from this vision.

In contrast, one of the possibilities Tao outlines for the field of mathematics — if an AI can simply solve mathematical problems at will — is that its goal is to help people understand and do math. This accomplishment is perhaps somewhat squishier than “solve a problem,” but only because it is more profound. It speaks to what we understand knowledge to be: not merely the collection of answers to questions, but the understanding of why those are the answers — a deeper way of connecting with the world and with ourselves. This sounds suspiciously like the humanities, doesn’t it?

Look, I am coming to believe we need a better quality of AI booster, because while I understand the Zuckerberg statement exists mostly to cheerlead Meta’s own AI investment, I have heard similar things coming from people who don’t have similar financial interests. Is the point of life merely to stockpile accomplishments? If that is what Silicon Valley believes, no wonder all the billionaires seem so unhappy all the time! They have traded experience for accomplishment, and cheated themselves out of their own lives in the process. They keep chasing more money and more power, because they think that will finally be enough — but as long as they do not experience things themselves, nothing will ever be enough.

What does it mean to live a good life?

When I am reading a book, or listening to music, or watching a movie, I am not just consuming a resource. I am experiencing other people’s minds. Artists have signature styles not merely as branding exercises but because they are expressing something about how they view the world, what they think beauty is, and what they believe to be the point of art. In prose, word choices are a kind of thumbprint for a specific person. In music, phrasing is another. In visual art, brush or pen strokes. Part of the point of the encounter is the aesthetic vision; the quality of another person’s attention. Part of it is your own attention: Does the artist’s aesthetic speak to you? What have you learned about your own aesthetics from it? What does beauty mean to you? What is pleasure?

If AI can do all the things we are promised it will do — hardly a given, but stick with me — then we are left with a question: What does using it accomplish? If you do not have to pay attention or do work to meet your goal, does your goal mean anything at all? In some ways, that throws us back to some of the oldest and most profound questions our species has encountered: What does it mean to live a good life? How do we love others? What does it mean to love ourselves?

Which brings me back to my climbing buddy’s motivational poster. What is there to say about something he did not create? It expresses very little of him. It took only seconds and required no attention, devotion, or even thought. The main thing I took away was that he requires a reminder to do cool shit — which, at least in my view, hardly requires a reminder at all.

Tech.title: Anker’s travel charger works in almost any country and is down to $20
Tech.content:
If you’ve got international travel coming up, an adapter is essential for keeping your phone, earbuds, power banks, and other gadgets charged. Anker’s Nano Travel Adapter is one of our picks from our guide to the best gadgets for summer travel because it can charge up to five devices at once, yet it’s small enough to fit in the palm of your hand. It’s also available in black for just $19.99 ($6 off) at Amazon, Best Buy, and directly from Anker (with code WS7DV2BNB82J) matching its best price to date.

The Nano’s four built-in sets of prongs should keep you covered in “over 200 countries and regions,” according to Anker. It also features two USB-C ports and two USB-A ports, along with an AC outlet for plugging in a standard wall charger. A single USB-C port delivers up to 20W, which should be enough to get an iPhone 17 to 50 percent in less than 30 minutes. That’s not enough power to charge most laptops, making the USB ports better suited for smaller gadgets like phones, tablets, earbuds, and power banks. You can still charge your laptop, however, by plugging its wall charger into the AC outlet.

What’s more, it’s designed to take up as little space as possible. The adapter’s only an inch thick with its prongs folded in and, at 3.8 ounces, weighs less than a smartphone. Just keep in mind that the Nano doesn’t convert voltage, so you’ll want to make sure gadgets like hair dryers and electric razors support the voltage at your destination before plugging them in.

Tech.title: Bluesky now lets you hide reposts from that annoying person you follow
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Bluesky has added a new feature that lets you hide reposts from a specific person in your feeds. The tool might be helpful if you want to stop seeing reposts from that one person who clogs up your feed with reposts of things you don’t care about. If you follow me, I may be that person, I’m sorry. I try not to be.

You can hide reposts from individual users by going to their profile, clicking the three dots button, and selecting the option to “Hide reposts in feeds.” (X offers a similar toggle.)

Bluesky also says that it’s launching a beta feature that will automatically add post numbers to threads. For long threads, it could be a useful way to get a sense of how much there might be to read, and it means you won’t have to manually add the numbers yourself. (Meta’s Threads already adds post counts to threads.) You can turn the feature on from Bluesky’s settings.

Tech.title: Costco’s great Switch 2 console bundle includes over $100 in free stuff
Tech.content:
Brad Bourque is a tech journalist and commerce writer based out of Portland, Oregon. He’s contributed to sites like Digital Trends, Business Insider, and WIRED.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The cost of the Nintendo Switch 2 is going up by $50 on September 1st, 2026, resulting in a $499.99 price tag for just the console. We’re just weeks away, but Costco is offering a fantastic $499.99 bundle for its members that includes a Nintendo Switch 2, a 256GB microSD Express card (usually $59), and a one year subscription to Nintendo Switch Online’s Expansion Pack tier, which normally costs $49.99 per year. That’s over $100 in value, and a great way to kickstart your Switch 2 experience.

The Switch 2 has 256GB of internal storage, so a microSD card is likely something you’ll need eventually for storing more games without having to constantly manage your library. With first-party Nintendo games typically running between 10 and 25GB, and larger third-party games reaching 50GB, a 256GB card should store anywhere from 5-20 additional games.

The Switch Online subscription includes a variety of features like cloud saving, online play, plus classic NES, SNES, and Game Boy titles. The Expansion Pack adds games from the GameCube, Game Boy Advance, N64, and Virtual Boy, and includes features for modern games, notably the Switch 2 upgrade packs for The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom.

Tech.title: What to expect from Google’s 2026 Pixel hardware launch event
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

It’s that time of year: On Wednesday, Google is set to host its annual Made by Google hardware launch event for Pixel gadgets. Google itself has already teased new slab-style and foldable Pixel smartphones, but leaks also indicate that the company could announce updated watches, a new color for familiar earbuds, and perhaps a brand new AirTag-like item tracker.

However, unusually, Google’s event is taking place in the evening: It kicks off on Wednesday at 6PM ET / 3PM PT instead of in the early afternoon or mid-morning, like many other tech events. And this time it has a celebrity host in Trevor Noah.

Even more strange: As noted by 9to5Google, the Google Store homepage has a Pixel 11 preorder countdown that will end at 10AM ET on Wednesday — which is many hours earlier than the launch event itself. That could mean that all of the details about Google’s new devices will be officially revealed long before the company hosts the formal launch event.

Here’s what we expect to see Google announce this week. If you want to watch the event live, you can catch it on YouTube.

The Pixel 11 lineup

A leaked marketing render of the Pixel 11 Pro Fold. Image: Evan Blass

Google has already hinted at its new phones while promoting the event, including shadowy glimpses of updated Pro and foldable phones. But the new smartphones could be largely iterative updates.

Google is expected to announce four new smartphones: the Pixel 11, the Pixel 11 Pro, the Pixel 11 Pro XL, and the Pixel 11 Pro Fold. Based on leaked images, they should look largely the same as the Pixel 10 lineup, though it appears they’ll have camera bars that are black all the way across and colors that might rule.

Perhaps the most notable visual difference will be a rainbow glowy light on the camera bar, which Google has already shown off for the Pixel 11 Pro. The company hasn’t yet specified what it’ll do or what it’s called. But code in Google’s contacts app spotted by 9to5Google indicates that it will be called “HiLight” and, at least for that contacts app, HiLight can be customized with different colors to indicate when certain people call you. Presumably, the light will work in some way with other apps as well. Based on a translation of a leaked Pixel 11 Pro Fold image, HiLight will also light up when you talk with Google’s Gemini AI.

A tease from Google showing the new light. Image: Google

Inside the phones, it seems likely that they’ll be powered by a new Tensor G6 chip. It’s rumored that the new chip will use TSMC’s 2nm process, which is expected to bring performance and power efficiency gains. If it does launch with a 2nm chip, the Pixel 11 series will be the first smartphones on the market to do so, and potentially by a hair; Apple’s chip for its next Pro phones that presumably launch in September is also expected to use the 2nm process.

Google is rumored to raise the starting storage of the base Pixel 11 and the base Pixel 11 Pro to 256GB, up from the 128GB floor with the Pixel 10 and Pixel 10 Pro. However, early Pixel 11 Pro listings have stated that the Pixel 11 Pro will have 12GB of RAM. If accurate, that would be down from the 16GB of RAM found in the Pixel 10 Pro lineup.

And expect the whole Pixel lineup to have a higher starting price, as a Google VP recently told 9to5Google that the Pixel family will get pricing “adjustments” due to the memory crisis.

The Pixel Watch 5

A leaked marketing render of the Pixel Watch 5. Image: OnLeaks and The Tide Chart

We already know that Google has manufactured at least one device called the Pixel Watch 5 thanks to, uh, Borderlands creator Randy Pitchford. In a May post that included two images, Pitchford said that a friend found the watch underwater while scuba diving. But recently, Google briefly teased the watch for an August 12th launch, so we should see more soon.

Leaked renders of the Pixel Watch 5 indicate that it may come in colors including black, polished silver, yellow gold, and a brass-y color, though the overall design looks quite similar to the Pixel Watch 4. Specs obtained by MyMobiles say that the new watch comes in 41 and 45mm screen sizes with battery life rated at 30 and 40 hours, respectively, matching the Pixel Watch 4. MyMobiles says that the Pixel Watch 5 will get 64GB of storage, which is double the 32GB of storage available previously.

On the software side, marketing materials obtained by MyMobiles suggest that Gemini Intelligence — which Google revealed earlier this year for Android phones — will be a big feature for the Pixel Watch 5 this year. One apparent marketing slide calls Gemini Intelligence a “personal, proactive assistant” that can proactively surface helpful information for you. A feature called “Proactive Suggestions” will also be able to help you reply to messages by recommending “context-aware replies” based on a conversation. The marketing materials also promise that the new watch will have Google’s “most accurate sleep tracking yet.”

However, like with the Pixel phones, expect higher prices. MyMobiles reports that the 41mm Wi-Fi model may start at $399, up from the Pixel Watch 4’s $349.99, while the 45mm Wi-Fi model could start at $429, up from $399.99.

The Pixel Buds Pro 2 in a new color

A leaked marketing render of new Pixel Buds. Image: Evan Blass

Google first launched the Pixel Buds Pro 2 in 2024, but two years on, it seems as if the company is just going to launch a new color instead of refreshing the product.

An apparent marketing image leaked by Evan Blass shows new earbuds in a nice olive green color that matches other renders that Blass and others have surfaced of the Pixel 11 lineup. But the headphones themselves otherwise look just like the Buds Pro 2 — and they have apparently already appeared on a Google Play rewards page with the name “Pixel Buds Pro 2.”

I guess there’s always next year for the Buds Pro 3.

The Pixel Tag item tracker

An image apparently showing off the Google Pixel Tag. Image: 9to5Google

Google may also launch something brand new: Pixel Tag, an AirTag-like item tracker. Based on an image 9to5Google recently obtained, it has an oval shape, meaning it could look a little bit different than Apple’s circular AirTag.

Presumably, the Pixel Tag will play nicely with Android’s Find Hub network. A machine translation of a now-removed online listing said the tracker will connect with the “Find My Device” network, which was the name of the network before Google changed it to Find Hub. But detailed specs and an expected price haven’t leaked just yet.

Don’t expect Googlebook laptops or smart glasses

Some leaks for new Googlebook laptops have also cropped up recently, but when it first announced the Googlebooks, Google said they would be launching in the fall. Google is also working on smart glasses and Android XR glasses, but those are scheduled for the fall, too.

Sure, Google could throw curveballs. But that hardware will probably get full reveals at a later date.

Tech.title: YouTube is making it harder to earn money on YouTube
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Starting February 1st, 2027, creators who want to monetize their channel through YouTube’s Partner Program (YPP) will need at least 1,000 subscribers and either 8,000 qualified watch hours over the past year, or 20 million qualified Shorts views in the last 90 days. That’s a sizeable jump from YouTube’s current requirement of 1,000 subscribers with 4,000 watch hours in the past year, or 1,000 subscribers with 10 million Shorts views in the last 90 days. Creators will also need to maintain 10 million Shorts views over 90 days to earn money from the Shorts Creators Pool, though falling below this threshold won’t result in removal from YPP.

Additionally, YouTube says creators will benefit from an expansion of its cheaper Premium Lite subscription, which is coming to all countries where it offers Premium. YouTube splits up subscription revenue to creators based on watch time and views, with 55 percent dedicated to long-form videos and 45 percent for Shorts. “With these additional subscribers, creators can expect higher earnings: when a user signs up for Premium, partners, on average, earn more than when the user was watching ads,” YouTube says.

The requirements are changing as YouTube ramps up efforts to become more like a premium TV service alongside Netflix, HBO Max, and Disney Plus, rather than just an online platform for videos. This year, YouTube struck deals to broadcast shows from big names like Trevor Noah, and broadly rolled out a feature that allows creators to organize their videos into seasons.

Separately, there are some new requirements for creators to keep earning money from ads and subscriptions through the YPP, though. That includes maintaining either 1,000 watch hours over the past year, 1 million Shorts views, or two long-form videos or five Shorts uploaded every 90 days. YouTube’s existing policies say it will remove creators from the YPP if they haven’t uploaded a video or published content to the Posts tab for at least six months. Creators already in the program will need to accept the new terms by January 31st, 2027, to keep making money from their content.

Tech.title: Four takeaways from Mark Zuckerberg’s massive AI manifesto
Tech.content:
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has a lot to say about the idealized future he now envisions for humanity co-existing with artificial intelligence — his latest essay spans more than 6,500 words on the matter. The lengthy manifesto Zuckerberg published on Monday, titled “The Future is for Everyone,” broadly lays out his beliefs about how the technology should be developed, expanded, and regulated, and how Meta is positioning itself to enable those goals.

Some points echo a similar (albeit, much shorter) public letter that Zuckerberg put out last year, heralding the importance of public access to superintelligent AI — a term for artificial general intelligence (AGI) models capable of surpassing human intelligence, which AI companies are racing to develop. Both were published with similar intentions: to pitch the supposed personal, societal, and economic benefits of superintelligent AI, and to grandstand Meta as a responsible steward to deliver that future.

Here are some of the main takeaways from Zuckerberg’s latest essay:

Sway the public on data centers

“Sustainable infrastructure development means that communities must benefit significantly from each project,” Zuckerberg said, detailing how Meta plans to resolve the ongoing PR crisis surrounding AI data center projects. This includes pledges to build energy-generating infrastructure “wherever we invest” that could potentially give low-cost energy back to the communities, and a commitment to “restore more water than we use in the watersheds where we operate by 2030.” Meta is also launching a Future Is For Everyone Fund to support local communities, and Zuckerberg says the company is providing free training and “guaranteed high-paying jobs” for skilled tradespeople in areas where Meta is building data centers.

Open AI for everyone

Meta is planning to focus its efforts on “delivering personal superintelligence to billions of people and small businesses,” arguing that doing so will empower everyone to become more entrepreneurial. Part of this involves offering the technology “for free or as affordably as possible,” and leaning into releasing more open source AI models that anyone can download. Doing so “will bring an abundance of personal agency, expression of ideas, deepening of relationships, economic and financial prosperity, improved health, and inventions we cannot imagine today,” according to Zuckerberg. He also says this will have an impact on “some aspects of the way we work,” but waves off concerns that AI will result in fewer jobs overall.

Less government oversight

Zuckerberg voices the importance of the US leading the open source AI ecosystem, citing concerns that competing models released by foreign labs “hold several advantages” because they face fewer training data restrictions. He pitches that the US needs to rethink policies around distillation and data use, arguing that while “some have tried to frame distillation as harmful,” the US will not be able to keep up if it keeps restricting AI models from learning from other models.

“I do not believe restricting access to foreign open source models is an effective solution,” said Zuckerberg. We should note here that these concerns are likely being voiced in response to the release of open-weight models from Chinese AI companies like Alibaba and Moonshot, which isn’t the same thing as being open-source, and the models Meta has released so far aren’t truly open-source either. He also espouses that access to personal superintelligence is essential for individuals to maintain their freedom, and should only be subject to restrictions “when truly required.”

But also, more government oversight

In cases where cybersecurity is involved, Zuckerberg proposes that frontier AI labs should work with the US government to help with bolstering critical infrastructure, and believes open-source AI models will improve system security over time — especially “once superintelligence enables most of the world’s code to be verifiably secure.” That plan includes pushing AI developers to share the training information of new models “for government use and review” intermediately instead of waiting until training has completed, which aligns with the Trump administration’s AI testing framework.

“This way the government will have early access to the most powerful models and an army of capable engineers to identify and patch security issues,” Zuckerberg said. “Labs should also work with law enforcement to help identify bad actors attempting to misuse their systems.”

Tech.title: Apple will stream Friday Night Baseball live in Vision Pro
Tech.content:

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Starting on Friday, August 28th, Apple will begin streaming Friday Night Baseball in immersive video on Apple Vision Pro. The stream will feature commentary from various analysts and reporters, and live graphics will be anchored around the viewers space during the game. After the games conclude, replays will be made available in the Apple TV app.
